facility.HQ.tema: The Centre — governance of the programme
facility.HQ.sommario: Management, scientific committee and coordination of the network.
facility.HQ.descrizione: Central Management coordinates the global network, the scientific committee and relations with funders. This is where priorities, budgets and the direction of the Sigma Programme are decided. It demands results, and it demands them soon.
facility.N1.tema: The Root — the programme's genetic memory
facility.N1.sommario: The cryobank and genomic archive from which the entire network descends.
facility.N1.descrizione: The first historic node of Eden Exotic, it safeguards the germline lines, the cryopreserved embryos and the genomic archive of every generation. It was here that Gen 1 of Protocol A was born, as a proof-of-concept. Nothing living is bred here: what is preserved is the possibility of doing it all over again from scratch. Staff call it «the root» because no site could exist without what is archived here.
facility.N1.specie: Germline lines, embryos and cryopreserved tissues of all species
facility.N2.tema: The Web — distributed perception and biomaterials
facility.N2.sommario: Distributed visual perception and high-performance silk biomaterials.
facility.N2.descrizione: Immersed in the forest around Iquitos, the site studies the extraordinary vision and problem-solving abilities of jumping spiders, together with the robustness of tarantulas. There are two main research lines: distributed visual perception — many independent optical sensors that together build a single representation of the environment — and silk-derived biomaterials, with applications in technical textiles and biomedical devices. It is a low-environmental-impact biomaterials centre that works in collaboration with local communities.
facility.N3.sommario: Rebuilding what is lost: tissue and limb regeneration.
facility.N3.descrizione: In the harsh climate of Hokkaidō it breeds amphibians capable of regenerating limbs and organs, with the axolotl as the keystone species. The site's goal is to translate this ability into regenerative medicine for humans, exploiting the regeneration genes conserved between amphibians and mammals. The colonies are fragile and require impeccable husbandry, which the staff ensure with some of the highest animal welfare standards in the network.
facility.N4.sommario: Comparative cognition programme and iguana behaviour.
facility.N4.descrizione: A sterile, geometric complex, designed for maximum control of experimental conditions. It runs the iguana cognition and behaviour programme, with standardised tests on learning, memory and problem-solving abilities. Among the specimens followed by the behavioural studies is 47B (4-07-B-ATC), enrolled in Protocol B. Marco Conti's team and the behaviourist Dominika Gradowska work here.
facility.N5.sommario: Venom biochemistry for antivenoms and therapies, with a supervised dual-use component.
facility.N5.descrizione: In the rains of the Western Ghats it breeds snakes in order to fractionate their venom and characterise its toxins. The isolated molecules become candidates for antidotes, analgesics and anticoagulants: this is pharmaceutical and antivenom research, conducted in a country where snakebites cause thousands of deaths a year. One component of the research is dual-use in nature and is managed under dedicated supervision, with the therapeutic candidates developed in India and the defence-relevant activities coordinated with Centre N.10.
facility.N5.specie: Snakes (elapids and viperids of the Western Ghats)
facility.N6.tema: The Body — strength, resilience, extreme environments
facility.N6.sommario: Monitor lizards engineered for strength, resilience and operation in extreme environments.
facility.N6.descrizione: In the Pripyat marshes it breeds enhanced monitor lizards — large, fast, strong and trainable for coordinated tasks — as part of the programme dedicated to physical strength, resilience and operation in extreme environments. Under the coordination of Col. Zaremba, the group of specimens (94G «Smok», 91F «Cień», 88G «Żubr» and the others) is the subject of applied study for the Sigma Programme, Eden Exotic's defence-oriented research line, within the prescribed validation procedures.
facility.N7.sommario: Salt, magnetism and long life: surviving and finding one's way in the ocean.
facility.N7.descrizione: Between Sulawesi and the Banda Sea it breeds marine reptiles and turtles to study their osmoregulation, long-distance navigation and exceptional longevity. Salt glands, magnetoreception and resilient telomeres are the three threads of research, with applications in human adaptation to water scarcity and hostile environments. It works closely with Biobank N.1 on the long-lived lines.
facility.N8.tema: The Mirror — camouflage and colour adaptation
facility.N8.sommario: A living screen: changing colour rapidly, between research and conservation.
facility.N8.descrizione: On the shores of Lake Victoria it combines a breeding facility and a field station to study chameleons and their rapid colour adaptation, both as signal and as camouflage. The site pursues two complementary programmes: a recognised conservation project for shrinking habitats, with reintroduction and monitoring of local populations, and applied research on chromatophores for the development of dynamically coloured surfaces. It is the only site in the network to combine husbandry and fieldwork.
facility.N9.sommario: The network's computational centre: genomic modelling and the cold-adaptation programme.
facility.N9.descrizione: In Kiruna, beyond the Arctic Circle, is Eden Exotic's computational centre: a data centre cooled by the Arctic climate that models the entire genomic network. It predicts the effects of gene edits, searches sequences for the signatures of emerging traits and runs the cold-adaptation programme. It houses no living specimens: it processes only genomic data and computational models in support of the other sites.
facility.N9.specie: No living species; genomic data and computational models
facility.N10.tema: The Trial — validation and operational integration
facility.N10.sommario: Validation, integration and security centre of the Sigma Programme.
facility.N10.descrizione: At an undisclosed location in the United States, it is the validation, operational integration and security centre of the Sigma Programme. Here the specimens and technologies developed at the other sites undergo applied validation in compliance with the security protocols. The Sigma Programme is Eden Exotic's dual-use research line, with stated purposes of defence, operation in extreme environments and rescue, conducted according to the responsible governance framework adopted by the company.
facility.N10.specie: No species of its own; integrates and validates specimens from other sites
facility.N11.tema: The Voice — avian communication and cognition
facility.N11.sommario: Avian cognition and bioacoustics programme: vocal mimicry and tool use.
facility.N11.descrizione: In New Caledonia, home of the tool-using crows, is the avian branch under construction: parrots for the study of vocal mimicry and sound production; corvids for tool use, problem-solving and the collective behaviours of the flock. The programme integrates bioacoustics and comparative cognition, with the goal of characterising the mechanisms of vocal communication and social intelligence in birds.
facility.N11.specie: Birds: corvids (New Caledonian crows) and parrots
facility.N12.tema: The Drought — life in arid conditions
facility.N12.sommario: New breeding facility under construction dedicated to reptiles adapted to hyper-arid environments.
facility.N12.descrizione: Construction of Breeding Facility N.12 is currently under way in the Namib Desert. The site will study osmoregulation and resistance to dehydration under hyper-arid conditions. The structures are designed to reproduce the desert's thermal and hygrometric regimes in a controlled way. Operational opening is expected once the works and health validations are complete.
facility.N13.tema: The Plateau — UV radiation and extreme stress
facility.N13.sommario: Research centre planned for the study of high-altitude environments with intense irradiation.
facility.N13.descrizione: Centre N.13 is an approved project, with opening planned for a future phase. The facility will focus on the effects of high altitude, intense ultraviolet radiation and large temperature swings. It will house no living species but will carry out environmental measurements and laboratory tests on samples and materials. The Atacama Desert was selected for its extreme and stable conditions.
facility.N13.specie: No living species; research station for extreme environments
facility.N15.sommario: Historic coastal site in the process of closure and consolidation of activities.
facility.N15.descrizione: Breeding Facility N.15 is being decommissioned. Its historic marine activities and lines are being consolidated into Breeding Facility N.7 in Indonesia. The transfer is taking place gradually, maintaining the chain of custody and health standards. When the process is complete, the site will cease breeding operations.
facility.N16.sommario: Second site of the Sigma Programme, dedicated to validation and operational trials, at an undisclosed location.
facility.N16.descrizione: Centre N.16 is the second site of the Sigma Programme, at an undisclosed location. It handles validation and integration of results, in coordination with Centre N.10. It has no species of its own and operates mainly on field trials and operational checks. The coordinates reported are approximate for reasons of confidentiality.
facility.N16.specie: No species of its own; validation and field trials
facility.LOG.tema: The Transit — quarantine and CITES handling
facility.LOG.sommario: Logistics hub for transfers, health quarantine and management of the CITES chain of custody.
facility.LOG.descrizione: The Logistics and Quarantine Centre serves as the hub for transfers between the network's sites. It manages health quarantine and the CITES chain of custody for international movement. Its port location in Rotterdam allows efficient connections to European and non-European facilities. The site breeds no species and does not appear on the map of operational nodes.
facility.REGAMER.tema: The Norm — regulatory affairs and alliances
facility.REGAMER.sommario: Office dedicated to regulatory affairs, intellectual property and partnerships in the Americas.
facility.REGAMER.descrizione: The Regulatory Affairs Office for the Americas handles relations with the region's competent authorities. It follows intellectual property, regulatory procedures and institutional and commercial partnerships. Its Boston location provides proximity to the main North American biotech hubs. The office performs administrative functions and houses no species.
facility.REGAPAC.sommario: Regional office for coordination, compliance and institutional relations in the Asia-Pacific area.
facility.REGAPAC.descrizione: The Asia-Pacific Regional Office coordinates the network's activities in the APAC area. It follows regulatory compliance and relations with local and regional institutions. Its Singapore location offers a central point of reference for the Asian and Oceanian sites. The office performs coordination functions and breeds no species.
facility.BIOPROD.tema: The Yield — from research to scale
facility.BIOPROD.sommario: Pilot plant under construction for the scale-up of biomaterials and research-derived compounds.
facility.BIOPROD.descrizione: The Bioproduction Pilot Plant is currently under construction in Cork. It will be dedicated to the scale-up of silk biomaterials, peptides and research-derived compounds. The plant will house no living species and will operate on controlled production processes. The goal is to translate laboratory results into pilot-scale volumes.
facility.BIOPROD.specie: No living species; scale-up of biomaterials and compounds
facility.ARCH.sommario: Cold backup copy of the germline lines and genomic data, in an Arctic environment.
facility.ARCH.descrizione: The Redundant Archive and Data Recovery holds a cold backup copy of Biobank N.1 and the genomic archive. The Arctic location of Svalbard guarantees stable low-temperature conditions and geographic redundancy. The facility preserves germline material and data, without housing any living species. The data recovery procedures ensure the continuity of the archive in the event of loss at the primary site.
facility.ARCH.specie: Redundant copy of germline lines and genomic data
facility.FIELD.sommario: Field station for work in Amazonia and the collection of wild references.
facility.FIELD.descrizione: The Amazonia Field Station carries out fieldwork and the regular collection of wild reference lines. It collaborates with Breeding Facility N.2 and Breeding Facility N.7 in sharing samples and biodiversity data. Its Manaus location offers logistical access to the Amazon basin. The facility breeds no species but operates as a base for field activities.
facility.FIELD.specie: Study and collection of wild reference lines
facility.ZERO.sommario: The company's first historic laboratory, now decommissioned.
facility.ZERO.descrizione: Site Zero was the company's first experimental laboratory. It was closed after Gen 1 and its material was transferred to Biobank N.1. The first lines developed here are now archived and preserved within the network. The site is no longer operational and retains only historical value.
facility.EXMARINE.tema: The Closure — activity consolidated into the network
facility.EXMARINE.sommario: Former pilot coastal station, decommissioned and merged into the network's marine programmes.
facility.EXMARINE.descrizione: The Former Marine Station was a pilot coastal station dedicated to the early studies on marine reptiles. It was decommissioned and its activities were merged into the network's marine programmes. Its Peniche location played a testing role in the early phases of the coastal work. The facility is no longer operational.
facility.EXMARINE.specie: Historic: early studies on marine reptiles
facility.VILLA.sommario: Private, confidential site for close behavioural study.
facility.VILLA.descrizione: A satellite facility of Breeding Facility N.4: a villa with humanities-style rooms upstairs and a modern laboratory below. A private and discreet site, wanted by Management to study the most interesting specimens up close, away from the main laboratory.
person.stern.bio: As Chief Executive Officer of Eden Exotic, Maria Stern sits at the head of HQ and coordinates the entire network of numbered facilities, from the germline laboratories of N.1 to the Sigma sites of N.10. She oversees corporate governance, scientific strategy and resource allocation, arbitrating between the priorities of research and the requirements of security and compliance. She approves budgets, decides which programmes to accelerate and sets the company's standards of responsibility and transparency.
person.stern.voce: She speaks with measured calm and terse sentences, authoritative without ever raising her voice, and chooses every word with precision.
person.stern.background: Trained in medicine and scientific management, she rose through translational research and the leadership of large biotech programmes before taking the helm of Eden Exotic.
person.conti.bio: Head of Protocol B at Breeding Facility N.4, Marco Conti leads the studies on the neural development and behavioural markers of the specimens. Day to day he designs the experimental cycles, analyses the neural markers and coordinates the group in interpreting the data on animal behaviour and cognition. His work focuses on identifying the biological conditions associated with cognitive development, studied with rigorous scientific method.
person.conti.voce: Enthusiastic and quick, he leaps eagerly from one hypothesis to the next, but always comes back to the experimental data.
person.conti.background: With a doctorate in neurobiology and years of research on brain plasticity, he came to Eden Exotic to study animal cognition with advanced experimental tools.
person.marini.bio: Geneticist of the Iguana Programme at Breeding Facility N.4, Elena Marini designs and validates the editing sequences and checks the gene expression data. She holds the research group to quantitative rigour, personally verifying the replicates before validating them. She is valued for her pragmatism and her attention to data quality control.
person.marini.voce: Concrete and direct, she brings discussions back to the data with precise questions, cordial but to the point.
person.marini.background: Trained in genetics at a public research institute, she moved to the private sector to work on large-scale gene editing programmes.
person.bianchi.bio: Molecular biologist of the Iguana Programme at Breeding Facility N.4, Paolo Bianchi characterises the genetic constructs and monitors off-target effects. He handles biosafety and biological risk assessment, promoting a methodologically cautious approach to running experiments. He is the voice that urges the group to consolidate results before moving on.
person.bianchi.voce: Calm and reflective, he frames his observations as questions and calls the group back to methodological caution.
person.bianchi.background: With a long path in molecular biology across universities and research centres, he joined Eden Exotic to contribute to the safety and rigour of the programme.
person.colombo.bio: PhD student of the Iguana Programme and the youngest member of the research group at Breeding Facility N.4, Alessandro Colombo assists the researchers in laboratory work: sample preparation, data processing and management of the experimental records. He brings energy and an ability to make original connections between data. He is a rising talent consolidating his experience within the group.
person.colombo.voce: Fast and exuberant, informal, he lights up when chasing a new idea.
person.colombo.background: A doctoral student in the biological sciences, he joined the Iguana Programme as a young researcher drawn to frontier research.
person.puddu.bio: Laboratory technician of the Iguana Programme at Breeding Facility N.4, Marina Puddu looks after the specimens day to day: feeding, hygiene of the enclosures, monitoring of parameters and observation. Her long experience and closeness to the animals make her especially attentive in documenting behaviour and promptly reporting any change to the researchers. She is a practical point of reference for the care of the specimens.
person.puddu.voce: Plain and warm, concrete in describing the animals and attentive to the details of their behaviour.
person.puddu.background: With technical training in animal science and years of hands-on experience in animal facilities, she is the day-to-day operational memory of the programme.
person.dominika.bio: Behaviourist of the Iguana Programme and in-house researcher at Breeding Facility N.4, Dominika Gradowska designs observation protocols, codes behavioural sequences and builds quantitative models to detect patterns in the specimen data. With an excellent memory and a keen ability to recognise patterns, she contributes to the group's behavioural analysis. Polish, she keeps meticulous and detailed records.
person.dominika.voce: Precise and intense, with a slight Polish accent, she alternates terse sentences with explanations rich in detail.
person.dominika.background: Trained in ethology and cognitive science in Poland, she joined Eden Exotic to apply her analytical skills to the study of animal behaviour.
person.monti.bio: Scientific Director and ethologist of Villa Monti, Professor Alfredo Monti leads the site's research and represents its academic profile. He studies the behaviour and cognition of the specimens with an ethological method and serves as scientific reference for the Monitor Lizard programme, as well as interlocutor with company management. He is known for his attention to animal welfare and his methodological rigour.
person.monti.voce: Cultured and patient, he speaks with the calm of someone who teaches and punctuates his talk with questions that invite thought.
person.monti.background: An academic with a long career in ethology, he brings his scientific experience to Eden Exotic for the close study of the specimens' behaviour.
person.adele.bio: Head of Security and Compliance at Villa Monti, Adele Ricci manages access, confidentiality protocols and information protection with rigorous precision. She acts as the interface between the site and the Sigma Programme, ensuring that exchanges take place in compliance with procedures and standards. Her role guarantees the correct and responsible handling of sensitive information.
person.adele.voce: Terse and controlled, she communicates orders and clarifications in short, precise sentences.
person.adele.background: She comes from a background in security and compliance with a rigorous approach, and is responsible for the interface between the Villa and the Sigma Programme.
person.pietro.bio: Pietro Visconti was a PhD student at the Villa Monti Laboratory, a brilliant researcher in theory and experimental design. He worked on experimental biology and the study of the specimens' cognition, with an ambitious approach to research. He left the laboratory following an accident that occurred during experimental work.
person.pietro.voce: Passionate and self-assured, he spoke of his work with enthusiasm and ambition.
person.pietro.background: A talented young researcher doing his doctorate at Villa Monti, he combined a solid theoretical grounding with a strong experimental spirit.
person.giancarlo.bio: Giancarlo is the long-serving assistant to the Scientific Directorate of Villa Monti. He manages Professor Monti's schedule, prepares materials and meetings and looks after archives and correspondence, knowing the organisation of the site inside out. He is a discreet and reliable presence, a point of reference for the daily running of the Villa.
person.giancarlo.voce: Courteous and measured, he answers with concision and discretion.
person.giancarlo.background: Long at Professor Monti's side, he has built his position on continuity and trust rather than on formal titles.
person.zaremba.bio: Colonel Stefan Zaremba commands Laboratory N.6, where the Monitor Lizard programme operates according to standards of military discipline. He coordinates units and handlers, assesses operational risks and ensures the link between scientific requirements and the chain of command. He is known for his rigour, integrity and attention to field safety.
person.zaremba.voce: Firm and sober, he gives clear orders with no words to spare, with a rigour that becomes almost formal courtesy.
person.zaremba.background: A long-serving officer with a career marked by integrity, he was placed in command of Laboratory N.6 to guarantee order and reliability for the Monitor Lizard programme.
person.nowak.bio: Unit veterinarian of the Monitor Lizard programme at Laboratory N.6, Wiktor Nowak looks after the health and welfare of the specimens: clinical examinations, nutrition, stress management and assessment of operational fitness. He works with the handlers to keep the specimens in good condition and is attentive to animal welfare. He is valued for his clinical competence and professional sensitivity.
person.nowak.voce: Gentle and reserved, precise and technical when he speaks of animal health.
person.nowak.background: A veterinarian trained in large-animal clinical practice, he was recruited for the Monitor Lizard programme for his expertise in reptiles.
person.gorski.bio: A non-commissioned officer and Handler-Alpha of the Monitor Lizard Unit at Laboratory N.6, Tomek Górski is the lead handler of the pack. A former dog handler, he applies a method built on a relationship developed over time: calm presence, consistent signals and trust earned day by day. He leads the training, assesses the state of the pack and translates operational needs into cues the specimens can understand.
person.gorski.voce: Warm and direct, he speaks of the specimens with a veteran's gruff affection, in a low, reassuring tone.
person.gorski.background: A former military dog handler, he brought to the Monitor Lizard programme a method based on relationship, becoming the unit's first Handler-Alpha.
person.sokol.bio: A sergeant and Backup Handler of the Monitor Lizard Unit at Laboratory N.6, Rafał Sokół assists Górski in handling the pack and is set to take over as Alpha. A former dog handler, he trains with the specimens and adopts the unit's relational methods, gradually building trust with the pack. He is valued for his dedication and operational adaptability.
person.sokol.voce: Restrained and measured, he says little about himself and much about the work, matter-of-factly.
person.sokol.background: A former dog handler, he was brought into the Monitor Lizard programme as a backup handler to prepare for the role of pack Alpha.
person.ursula-brunner.ruolo: Director of the Biobank and head of the genetic archive
person.ursula-brunner.bio: Director of the Biobank at Breeding Facility N.1, Ursula Brunner has devoted twenty years to building Eden Exotic's catalogue of germline lines. She oversees the cataloguing, preservation and integrity of thousands of samples, with great attention to completeness and traceability. A Basel geneticist, she is the guarantor of the quality of the company's genetic archive.
person.ursula-brunner.voce: Precise and sober, with a Swiss-German accent, she speaks of the samples as a heritage to be preserved.
person.ursula-brunner.background: A geneticist trained in Basel, she built the biobank of Breeding Facility N.1 from scratch and has tied her entire career to it.
person.dr-matthias-vogel.bio: Chief cryo-curator at Breeding Facility N.1, Matthias Vogel is a materials physicist specialised in ultra-low-temperature preservation, responsible for the liquid nitrogen tanks. He checks levels, thermal gradients and sensors, calibrates the alarms and plans redundancies to guarantee the stability of the samples. His background in physics brings a rigorous engineering approach to the management of cryogenic risk.
person.dr-matthias-vogel.voce: Methodical and concrete, he explains everything in terms of temperatures, margins and tolerances.
person.dr-matthias-vogel.background: A materials physicist by training, he moved into preservation biology, bringing engineering precision to cryogenics.
person.helena-roth.bio: Germline geneticist at Breeding Facility N.1, Helena Roth reconstructs and stabilises the Gen 1 lines, the founding genetic heritage of the programme. She repairs degraded sequences, checks genomic stability and documents every intervention with precision. Her work is oriented towards preserving the integrity of the germline lines.
person.helena-roth.voce: Measured and precise, technical and careful in her choice of words.
person.helena-roth.background: A geneticist specialised in germline lines, she works at Breeding Facility N.1 on reconstructing the founding Gen 1 lines.
person.dr-lukas-ammann.bio: Genomic archivist and CITES traceability officer at Breeding Facility N.1, Lukas Ammann manages the register that links each specimen to its genetic sample. He verifies matches, updates the legal documentation and safeguards the chain of custody, essential to the programme's international compliance. He is known for his meticulousness and documentary rigour.
person.dr-lukas-ammann.voce: Meticulous and formal, he cites procedures and regulatory references with precision.
person.dr-lukas-ammann.background: Specialised in genetic documentation management and protected-wildlife regulation, he brings long experience in CITES traceability and compliance.
person.corinne-frei.bio: Quality and compliance manager at Breeding Facility N.1, Corinne Frei is a former pharmaceutical inspector who brings high standards of procedural quality to the programme. She drafts and reviews protocols, conducts internal audits and documents every deviation, ensuring the compliance of the facility's processes. She is rigorous and attentive to adherence to standard operating procedures.
person.corinne-frei.voce: Formal and precise, she speaks in terms of procedures and requirements, courteous but inflexible when something is non-compliant.
person.corinne-frei.background: A former inspector in the pharmaceutical sector, she moved to Eden Exotic bringing rigorous quality standards to the oversight of Breeding Facility N.1.
person.dr-ricardo-vasquez-chavez.bio: Director of N.2, Ricardo coordinates the Amazonian station dedicated to salticid spiders and tarantulas, which combines research on perception, silk production and relations with the communities of Iquitos. His days are divided between meetings with funders, review of genetic protocols and inspection of the colonies in the climate-controlled terrarium. He is committed to bringing skilled research and employment to Amazonia, responsibly managing the applications of the biomaterials developed by the facility.
person.dr-ricardo-vasquez-chavez.voce: He speaks with a director's calm and diplomacy, alternating regional pride with institutional caution about end applications.
person.dr-ricardo-vasquez-chavez.backgro: Peruvian, trained in biology in Lima and specialised in arachnology abroad, he returned to Amazonia after years of academic career to run a facility that would combine science and local development.
person.ana-maria-rios.bio: Ana María studies the tetrachromatic vision and problem-solving abilities of the jumping spiders of N.2, designing small mazes and choice tests to understand how they plan an ambush. She spends hours at the microscope and analysing slow-motion footage, noting every eye movement and every calculated jump. She is fascinated by the idea of a «web that sees» and by the sophisticated visual perception of these spiders.
person.ana-maria-rios.voce: Enthusiastic and meticulous, she lights up describing details and uses visual metaphors.
person.ana-maria-rios.background: A Peruvian ethologist with a doctorate in animal behaviour, she came to N.2 drawn by the chance to study salticid cognition with tools no university could afford.
person.ing-julio-herrera.ruolo: Head of biomaterials and silk production
person.ing-julio-herrera.bio: Julio is the engineer working to take spider silk from laboratory scale to industrial scale, with recombinant fibres, wet spinning and tensile testing. For N.2 he represents the branch of biomaterials and intellectual property: lightweight, strong materials that could replace polluting fibres. He sees patents as an opportunity for technological development for Peru.
person.ing-julio-herrera.voce: Pragmatic and enthusiastic like an engineer, he talks in terms of performance, costs and patents.
person.ing-julio-herrera.background: A Peruvian materials engineer, after experience in the textile and polymer industry he moved to biomaterials research, looking for a project that combined sustainability and commercial value.
person.ing-julio-herrera.competenze: Spinning and mechanical properties of fibres
person.carla-tuesta.bio: Carla is the geneticist who applies Protocols C and D to the salticids, introducing targeted modifications with extreme caution and carefully documenting every step. Her days are made of sequencing, cell cultures and careful re-reading of the data. She is known for her scientific caution and the meticulousness of her experimental documentation.
person.carla-tuesta.voce: Measured and cautious, she chooses her words carefully and keeps a professional tone.
person.carla-tuesta.background: A Peruvian geneticist trained between Lima and a doctorate abroad, she joined N.2 to work on the genome editing of jumping spiders.
person.manuel-shapiama.bio: Manuel is the field technician of N.2, raised in the forest and able to spot jumping spiders and tarantulas where others see only bark and leaves. He organises the collection outings, prepares the containers and passes on to the researchers the practical knowledge of the jungle, from the safe trails to the species to be respected. He procures the wild specimens the laboratory needs and is an indispensable resource for fieldwork.
person.manuel-shapiama.voce: He speaks plainly and concretely, full of references to the forest.
person.manuel-shapiama.background: A Peruvian of indigenous Amazonian origin, he learned the forest from his family before becoming a field technician for the station, where his practical knowledge is indispensable.
person.dr-haruki-tanaka.bio: Director of N.3, Haruki leads the Japanese station dedicated to amphibians and in particular to the axolotl, coordinating research on regeneration, veterinary care and genetic protocols. His days begin early, with a check of the tanks, and continue amid data review and calls for experimental caution. He is convinced that understanding amphibian regeneration can contribute to human medicine.
person.dr-haruki-tanaka.voce: Calm and reflective, with a controlled idealism; he speaks of regeneration as a promise for medicine.
person.dr-haruki-tanaka.background: A herpetologist from Hokkaidō, after an academic path across Japan and international collaborations he chose to devote his career to the axolotl as a key to regenerative medicine.
person.yumi-sato.bio: Yumi studies how salamanders and newts rebuild lost limbs, tails and tissues, reconstructing step by step the cellular sequence of regeneration. She spends her days amid blastema cultures, microscopy and time-lapse observations. Her work aims to translate the regenerative mechanisms of amphibians into prospects for human medicine.
person.yumi-sato.voce: Intense and determined, she often links the science to its possible impact on people.
person.yumi-sato.background: A Japanese biologist specialised in regenerative medicine, she has directed her research towards amphibians and the mechanisms of tissue regrowth.
person.dr-kenji-nakamura.bio: Kenji is the geneticist of N.3 who studies the regeneration genes shared between amphibians and mammals, searching for the molecular circuits active in axolotls and silent in humans. He works between comparative genome analyses and expression experiments, and in meetings he often asks for more data before proceeding. He is the guarantor of the group's experimental caution.
person.dr-kenji-nakamura.voce: Analytical and cautious, he speaks in terms of conditions and reservations; he is the voice that calls for prudence.
person.dr-kenji-nakamura.background: A Japanese geneticist with a solid grounding in comparative genomics, he joined N.3 to study the molecular basis of regeneration across different species.
person.aiko-ishikawa.bio: Aiko is the veterinarian responsible for the welfare of the amphibian colonies of N.3, extremely fragile organisms sensitive to any variation in temperature, water quality or stress. She monitors the parameters, treats skin infections and refines the husbandry standards, convinced that healthy animals produce reliable science. She firmly defends the breeding conditions.
person.aiko-ishikawa.voce: Firm and protective, with a practical clinical tone; attentive to animal welfare.
person.aiko-ishikawa.background: A Japanese veterinarian specialised in exotic and laboratory animals, she chose amphibians for the clinical challenge posed by their delicate needs.
person.sora-yoshida.bio: Sora is the breeding technician of N.3, responsible for the daily survival of the amphibians: he manages tanks, filters, moulting cycles and feeding with great precision. He knows every sound of the pumps and every nuance of the water, intervening before the sensors even flag a problem. His practical expertise is essential to the facility's colonies.
person.sora-yoshida.voce: Sober and concrete, he speaks in terms of tasks and routines, with quiet dedication.
person.sora-yoshida.background: A Japanese technician with experience in aquaculture and terrarium keeping, he joined N.3 to manage the breeding conditions of the research amphibians.
person.sora-yoshida.competenze: Management of tanks and moulting cycles
person.dr-arjun-nair.bio: Director of N.5, Arjun leads the Indian station dedicated to snakes, where venom research ranges from life-saving antidotes to defence applications. His days are divided between the serpentarium, the biochemistry laboratories and the coordination of institutional relations. He presents the programme as antivenom and drug research, complemented by a responsibly managed dual-use component.
person.dr-arjun-nair.voce: Reflective and articulate, he argues with logic and attention to the ethical implications of the work.
person.dr-arjun-nair.background: A herpetologist from Kerala, trained in India and specialised in snake biology, he came to lead N.5 driven by the ambition to develop better antivenoms for the subcontinent.
person.priya-menon.bio: Priya is the venom biochemist of N.5, who fractionates toxins, maps peptides and identifies the molecules with therapeutic potential against pain, hypertension or clots. For her, every venom is a pharmacopoeia evolved over millions of years, a collection of molecular keys to be studied with respect. Her work feeds the search for drugs derived from toxins.
person.priya-menon.voce: Precise and passionate about molecules, almost lyrical when she speaks of toxins as drugs.
person.priya-menon.background: An Indian biochemist with a doctorate in molecular pharmacology, she chose the study of venoms for their extraordinary therapeutic potential.
person.dr-vikram-deshpande.bio: Vikram is the pharmacologist who translates the toxins characterised by his colleagues into therapeutic candidates, designing efficacy assays, dose studies and toxicity profiles. His days are made of dose-response curves, cellular models and planning of the development pipelines for potential drugs. He represents the pharmacological and translational branch of the programme.
person.dr-vikram-deshpande.voce: Methodical and precise, he readily talks about therapies and mechanisms of action.
person.dr-vikram-deshpande.background: An Indian pharmacologist with experience in the drug industry, he moved to N.5 drawn by the therapeutic potential of toxins and the research freedom the facility offers.
person.lakshmi-iyer.ruolo: Herpetologist and head of the serpentarium
person.lakshmi-iyer.bio: Lakshmi is the herpetologist who cares for the snakes of the N.5 serpentarium, handling them with great skill and respect. She manages feeding, moulting, quarantines and breeding, knowing the temperament of each specimen. She joined the programme for the conservation of the endemic species of the Western Ghats.
person.lakshmi-iyer.voce: Calm and respectful, she speaks of the snakes with expertise and attention to their dignity.
person.lakshmi-iyer.background: An Indian herpetologist passionate about biodiversity, she came to N.5 with the motivation of conserving the endemic snakes of the Western Ghats.
person.suresh-gowda.bio: Suresh is the technician in charge of venom extraction at N.5, a craft he has practised for twenty years with calm and confidence. He immobilises the snakes, collects the venom on the glass and freeze-dries it with precise, efficient movements. His long practical experience makes him a key figure in the venom production chain.
person.suresh-gowda.voce: Laconic and concrete, he speaks in terms of practical experience and proverbs about the trade.
person.suresh-gowda.background: An Indian technician from Karnataka with decades of practical experience in venom extraction, he learned the trade in the field more than from books.
person.dr-bagus-wijaya.bio: Director of N.7, Bagus leads the Indonesian station dedicated to marine reptiles and turtles, with research on osmoregulation, navigation and longevity. His days are divided between the coastal tanks, the sea campaigns and institutional relations. He is driven by a strong interest in marine ecosystems and in the contribution that understanding them can make to conservation.
person.dr-bagus-wijaya.voce: Affable and passionate, he speaks with enthusiasm about the sea and longevity.
person.dr-bagus-wijaya.background: A marine biologist from Sulawesi, he built his career studying Indonesia's coastal ecosystems before taking over the direction of N.7.
person.sri-wulandari.bio: Sri studies how marine reptiles and turtles survive in salt water, focusing on the salt glands and the fine mechanisms of osmoregulation. She spends her days amid blood sampling, electrolyte measurements and water-balance models. She imagines how these adaptations might inspire solutions for water scarcity in a warming world.
person.sri-wulandari.voce: Reflective and future-oriented, she often links reptile physiology to the great themes of the human water crisis.
person.sri-wulandari.background: An Indonesian physiologist specialised in the adaptations of marine animals, she came to N.7 interested in survival strategies in saline environments.
person.dr-yusuf-maulana.bio: Yusuf studies how sea turtles find their way across thousands of kilometres of ocean, returning to the exact beach where they were born. His days are made of satellite data, magnetic-field experiments and observations of newly hatched young orienting towards the sea. He is fascinated by magnetoreception, the ability to sense the Earth's magnetic field as a map and a compass at once.
person.dr-yusuf-maulana.voce: Curious and enthusiastic, he readily loses himself in fascinated explanations of biological compasses and magnetic maps.
person.dr-yusuf-maulana.background: An Indonesian biologist specialised in animal behaviour and orientation, he joined N.7 drawn by the mystery of sea turtle navigation.
person.ni-made-ayu.bio: Ni Made is the longevity geneticist of N.7, who works on Protocol H studying turtles and specimens with extraordinarily slow ageing. She spends her days amid telomere analyses, senescence markers and comparisons between young and long-lived individuals. She searches for the genes that slow biological time.
person.ni-made-ayu.voce: Brilliant and passionate, she speaks of ageing as a scientifically tractable problem.
person.ni-made-ayu.background: An Indonesian geneticist, probably Balinese, specialised in the biology of ageing, she came to N.7 to study the extremely long-lived marine animals.
person.hasan-lampe.bio: Hasan is the marine field technician of N.7, a former fisherman of the Banda Sea who turned his knowledge of the sea into a profession within the station. He manages the coastal tanks, organises the at-sea retrievals and pilots the boats with the confidence of someone who has spent his life on the water. He knows the currents, the tides and the animals' behaviour, and is a reference point for fieldwork.
person.hasan-lampe.voce: Blunt and practical, he speaks with the authority of a man of the sea, mixing a fisherman's experience with gruff affection for the animals.
person.hasan-lampe.background: An Indonesian former fisherman of the Banda Sea, he put his seafaring experience at the service of N.7 as a field technician.
person.dr-joseph-okello.ruolo: Director of the Breeding Facility and field station
person.dr-joseph-okello.bio: Director of N.8, Joseph leads the Ugandan station dedicated to chameleons, which combines research on camouflage, chromatophore genetics and a solid field conservation programme. His days alternate between running the station, outings into the local forests and institutional meetings. He places great emphasis on the conservation component of the project and on the protection of threatened species.
person.dr-joseph-okello.voce: Confident and strategic, he speaks eloquently of conservation and research.
person.dr-joseph-okello.background: A Ugandan zoologist trained between Kampala and international institutions, he built his career combining research and conservation of East African wildlife.
person.grace-nakato.bio: Grace studies the colour adaptation of chameleons, investigating how the chromatophores and photonic crystals of the skin produce colour changes for communication, thermoregulation and camouflage. She spends her days amid behavioural observations, skin spectrophotometry and analysis of how the animal actively controls its own livery. She describes the chameleon as a «living screen», a surface that processes and displays information.
person.grace-nakato.voce: Wonder-struck and descriptive, she uses vivid images such as «living screen».
person.grace-nakato.background: A Ugandan biologist specialised in physiology and behaviour, she devoted herself to chameleons drawn by the mechanisms of their colour change.
person.dr-samuel-mugisha.ruolo: Field ecologist and head of conservation
person.dr-samuel-mugisha.bio: Samuel is the field ecologist of N.8, who divides his time between the station and the increasingly fragmented Ugandan forests where the chameleons live. He conducts censuses, maps habitats, monitors populations and works with Eden to channel resources into concrete conservation. He knows the local rural communities, aware that habitat protection depends on their involvement.
person.dr-samuel-mugisha.voce: Concrete and passionate about the land, he speaks of forests and communities with urgency; pragmatic about conservation.
person.dr-samuel-mugisha.background: A Ugandan ecologist committed to conservation, he chose to collaborate with N.8 to access resources useful for protecting the threatened forest habitats.
person.aisha-namuli.bio: Aisha is the young geneticist of N.8 who applies Protocols B and C to the chameleons' chromatophores, studying and modifying the genes that regulate skin colour. Her days are made of gene editing, expression analysis and cell cultures, pursued with energy and ambition. She is a talented researcher focused on the technical challenge.
person.aisha-namuli.voce: Energetic and ambitious, she speaks with technical confidence and youthful drive.
person.aisha-namuli.background: A talented young Ugandan geneticist trained in molecular biology, she joined N.8 seeing it as an exceptional career opportunity.
person.peter-ssemwanga.bio: Peter is the field technician of N.8, responsible for the terrariums and the camera traps that document the chameleons both in captivity and in the wild. He builds and maintains the artificial habitats, sees to the feeding and retrieves the trap images with the patience of someone who knows the slow rhythms of these animals. He knows every specimen in the terrarium closely and is an essential support to the observational work.
person.peter-ssemwanga.voce: Warm and descriptive, he speaks of the chameleons with affection and attention to detail.
person.peter-ssemwanga.background: A local Ugandan technician, he learned reptile care and terrarium management in the field, becoming indispensable to N.8.
person.astrid-lindqvist.ruolo: Director of the Centre and head of bioinformatics
person.astrid-lindqvist.bio: Director of Centre N.9 in Kiruna, Astrid Lindqvist leads a data centre that models the entire genomic network of Eden Exotic. She coordinates bioinformaticians and engineers, sets the priorities of the models and integrates the data coming from all the facilities. Her goal is to turn data into tools for understanding the biology of the specimens.
person.astrid-lindqvist.voce: Lucid and reflective, she explains complex systems with clarity.
person.astrid-lindqvist.background: A bioinformatician of Nordic training, she built the computing centre she now directs in Kiruna, at the crossroads of data and biology.
person.dr-erik-johansson.ruolo: Head of machine learning and data science
person.dr-erik-johansson.bio: Head of ML and data science at Centre N.9, Erik Johansson builds the neural networks that predict the effect of a gene edit before it is carried out. He trains models, optimises the metrics and validates the predictions against experimental data. His work makes the design of genetic interventions more efficient and targeted.
person.dr-erik-johansson.voce: Analytical and enthusiastic about models, he speaks in terms of metrics and architectures.
person.dr-erik-johansson.background: A data scientist specialised in machine learning, he joined Centre N.9 to apply machine learning to genomic prediction.
person.maja-bergstrom.bio: Computational genomicist at Centre N.9, Maja Bergström analyses the specimens' genomes to identify the genetic basis of emerging physiological traits. She compares sequences, identifies conserved regions and correlates genetic variants with the observed characteristics. She is driven by a keen scientific curiosity about the genetics of complex traits.
person.maja-bergstrom.voce: Curious and passionate, she lights up recounting patterns and correlations.
person.maja-bergstrom.background: A researcher in computational genomics, she came to Centre N.9 to study the genetic basis of emerging physiological traits.
person.dr-nils-andersson.ruolo: Head of infrastructure and the data centre
person.dr-nils-andersson.bio: Head of infrastructure and the data centre at Centre N.9, Nils Andersson manages the physical machine on which all of Eden Exotic's genomic modelling runs. He looks after servers, cooling, power and operational continuity, exploiting the cold Lapland climate to dissipate the heat of the computing halls. He guarantees the reliability and energy efficiency of the infrastructure.
person.dr-nils-andersson.voce: Practical and concrete, he talks about power, cooling and reliability.
person.dr-nils-andersson.background: An IT infrastructure engineer, he designed and manages the data centre of Centre N.9, exploiting the Arctic climate for cooling.
person.sofia-kallio.bio: Head of the cold-adaptation programme at Centre N.9, Sofia Kallio models the mechanisms that make organisms tolerant to low temperatures. She studies antifreeze proteins, cellular responses to freezing and strategies of natural cryoprotection. Her research has applications for resistance to extreme environments.
person.sofia-kallio.voce: Serene and enthusiastic, she speaks of cold and adaptation with an almost lyrical affection.
person.sofia-kallio.background: A biologist specialised in adaptations to low temperatures, she found in Centre N.9 the ideal place to study freeze tolerance.
person.col-ris-james-whitaker.ruolo: Director of the Centre and head of the Sigma Programme
person.col-ris-james-whitaker.bio: Director of site N.10 and of the Sigma Programme, retired colonel James Whitaker leads the dual-use component of Eden Exotic. He coordinates the validations, the relations with clients and the operational priorities of the programme, oriented towards the development of resilient biological systems for applications in defence, extreme environments and rescue. He runs the programme according to criteria of responsibility, oversight and preparedness.
person.col-ris-james-whitaker.voce: Sober and firm, he speaks in terms of objectives and readiness, with the composure of an experienced officer.
person.col-ris-james-whitaker.background: A retired officer with long operational experience, he directs site N.10, bringing to the Sigma Programme a mindset oriented towards preparedness and protection.
person.dr-daniel-cole.bio: Head of field validation at site N.10, Daniel Cole assesses and certifies the operational fitness of the specimens through tests, metrics and protocols. He designs the trials, collects the performance data and documents the results according to rigorous criteria. He is known for his methodological precision and his attention to protocols.
person.dr-daniel-cole.voce: Technical and precise, he speaks in terms of metrics and protocols, with attention to method.
person.dr-daniel-cole.background: A validation and testing specialist with operational experience, he was brought into site N.10 to certify the specimens according to the criteria of the Sigma Programme.
person.rebecca-hayes.bio: Head of operational security at site N.10, Rebecca Hayes protects the Sigma Programme from information leaks and intrusions. She manages access, confidentiality protocols, counter-intelligence and vulnerability assessment, ensuring that the programme operates in a secure and controlled setting. She is careful and rigorous in protecting sensitive information.
person.rebecca-hayes.voce: Firm and vigilant, she speaks in terms of risks and countermeasures, cordial and attentive.
person.rebecca-hayes.background: A security professional with experience in sensitive environments, she safeguards site N.10 to protect the Sigma Programme from undue exposure.
person.marcus-bennett.ruolo: Head of operational integration and defence liaison
person.marcus-bennett.bio: Head of operational integration and defence at site N.10, Marcus Bennett is the point of contact between Eden Exotic and the institutional clients of the Sigma Programme. He looks after relations, prepares presentations and negotiates agreements, explaining the dual-use nature of the programme and its protective applications. He is skilled in communication and in developing institutional relations.
person.marcus-bennett.voce: Confident and persuasive, he speaks in terms of opportunities and benefits, affable and reassuring.
person.marcus-bennett.background: A professional in development and institutional relations with experience in the defence sector, he serves as the interface between Eden and the clients of the Sigma Programme.
person.karen-foster.ruolo: Head of dual-use ethics and compliance
person.karen-foster.bio: Head of dual-use ethics and compliance at site N.10, Karen Foster oversees the ethical assessment of the Sigma Programme's activities. She reviews proposals, drafts opinions and takes part in the decision-making forums as a voice of governance, ensuring that dual-use research is carried out within responsible limits. Her role guarantees the ethical oversight of the programme.
person.karen-foster.voce: Argumentative and considered, she weighs every case scrupulously and with attention to implications.
person.karen-foster.background: An expert in ethics and compliance with training in the governance of sensitive research, she safeguards the ethical framework of the dual-use Sigma Programme at site N.10.
person.dr-etienne-lefevre.bio: Designated Director of N.11, Étienne is a French neuroethologist called upon to set up the avian branch dedicated to corvids and parrots, devoted to the study of non-human language and cognition. In this start-up phase he handles the design of the aviaries, the recruitment of the team and the definition of the research protocols. He is fascinated by communication across different species and by the cognitive abilities of birds.
person.dr-etienne-lefevre.voce: Elegant and diplomatic, he speaks as a scholar of language and cognition.
person.dr-etienne-lefevre.background: A French neuroethologist trained in the cognitive and behavioural sciences, he was designated to launch the avian branch of N.11 in New Caledonia.
person.marie-wamytan.bio: Marie is a Kanak ornithologist who studies the corvids of N.11, in particular the extraordinary cognitive and tool-use abilities of the New Caledonian crows. She spends her days amid field observations, cognitive experiments and care of the birds, a species from her own archipelago. She joined the programme with a strong conservation motivation.
person.marie-wamytan.voce: Rooted and passionate, she speaks of the crows with Kanak identity pride.
person.marie-wamytan.background: A Kanak ornithologist from New Caledonia, she studied the birdlife of her own archipelago and joined N.11 to protect the endemic corvids.
person.dr-julien-moreau.ruolo: Head of bioacoustics and vocal mimicry
person.dr-julien-moreau.bio: Julien studies the bioacoustics and vocal mimicry of parrots, investigating how they manage to reproduce practically any voice with impressive fidelity. His days are made of recordings, spectrograms and analysis of the neural control of song, in search of the mechanisms that make a bird capable of reproducing a human timbre. He describes this ability as «the gift of speaking with someone else's mouth».
person.dr-julien-moreau.voce: Fascinated and curious, he uses evocative images such as «speaking with someone else's mouth».
person.dr-julien-moreau.background: A French bioacoustician specialised in vocal production and imitation in birds, he joined N.11 to study the extraordinary mimicry of parrots.
person.lea-poadja.bio: Léa studies behaviour and identity in birds, in particular how corvids and parrots recognise and imitate individuals, distinguishing a companion from a stranger or one voice from another. She spends her days amid recognition experiments, vocal playbacks and analysis of the birds' social networks. She is fascinated by how an avian mind builds the concept of identity.
person.lea-poadja.voce: Curious and sensitive, she speaks with enthusiasm about identity and recognition.
person.lea-poadja.background: A researcher from New Caledonia specialised in animal behaviour, she came to N.11 interested in individual recognition and identity in birds.
person.paul-nechero.bio: Paul is the aviary technician of N.11, a local Kanak who builds, adapts and maintains the aviaries in which the corvids and parrots live. He designs structures that respect the birds' needs, sees to the feeding and environmental enrichment and observes his charges with an attention rooted in the local culture. For him, the care of the aviaries is a work of responsibility and respect.
person.paul-nechero.voce: Quiet and respectful, he speaks of the birds with a reverence rooted in Kanak culture, without superfluous technicalities.
person.paul-nechero.background: A Kanak technician from New Caledonia, he combined the traditional knowledge of his own land with the practical care of the aviaries of N.11.
specimen.47B.note: Reference specimen of the Cognition & Behaviour programme (Protocol B). Under extended behavioural study at Villa Monti for certain atypical responses, still being characterised and not replicated under controlled conditions.
specimen.41C.note: Sensory counter-check for Protocol C: enhancement of UV vision and vomeronasal olfaction, behavioural profile typical of the species.
specimen.49B.note: Same edit package of Protocol B (B-ATC) as 47B; behavioural profile within the norm for the species. Serves as a protocol control.
specimen.37B.note: Historic third-generation baseline, profile typical of the species. Pre-cohort reference for Protocol B.
specimen.26B.note: Second-generation specimen with inconclusive behavioural observations that were never replicated; died before characterisation. Material preserved in the biobank (N.1).
specimen.53D.note: Fifth-generation specimen (Protocol D) deemed unsuitable for standard husbandry and transferred out; CITES traceability incomplete due to a documentation error.
specimen.94G.note: Dominant male of the cohort, powerful build and high coordination within the group. Reference for Protocol G.
specimen.91F.note: Shy specimen of Protocol F (metabolic dormancy), with particularly stable controlled torpor.
specimen.88G.note: Specimen of exceptional size, high bone density and endurance. Docile to handling.
specimen.96G.note: Young female of reduced size and very fast; exploratory behaviour under study.
specimen.85F.note: Protocol F (metabolic dormancy), marked tolerance to extreme cold.
specimen.89G.note: Veteran adult specimen of the cohort, reference musculoskeletal parameters.
specimen.11C.note: First salticid line with the acuity of the principal eyes extended into the near ultraviolet. Discriminates reflectance patterns on motionless prey at twice the distance of the wild strain. Sensory baseline of cohort C.
specimen.12D.note: Haemolymph enriched with antimicrobial peptides that reduces mortality from fungal infection in captivity. Survives exposures to Ophiocordyceps spores that are lethal in the controls.
specimen.21C.note: Increased density of photoreceptors in the layered retina. Better colour separation in the green-red range, useful for assessing the transfer of the sensory trait between broods.
specimen.22D.note: Control strain for resistance to entomopathogenic nematodes; faster cellular immune response but unchanged fecundity.
specimen.31C.note: Individual notable for an extremely low motion-detection threshold. No sign of behavioural flexibility beyond the predatory repertoire typical of salticids.
specimen.32D.note: Cohort proposed to combine fungal and bacterial resistance in a single haemocyte profile. Under evaluation for trait stability across moults.
specimen.11B.note: Founding line with accelerated limb regeneration and thermal tolerance up to 24 °C without loss of neoteny. Fibrosis-free epidermal healing even at elevated temperatures.
specimen.12G.note: Blastema formation 30% faster after amputation of the forelimb. Reference individual for longitudinal imaging of regeneration.
specimen.21B.note: Pigmented dermal regeneration: the colour motifs are faithfully reconstituted after injury. Useful for studying the restoration of the melanophore pattern.
specimen.22G.note: Selected for cardiac tissue regeneration after controlled ventricular injury, in addition to limb regrowth. Model for scar-free myocardial repair.
specimen.31B.note: Stable neoteny over three generations with reliable suppression of metamorphosis. Combines regeneration and thermal stress resistance; candidate for cryopreserved transfer to N1.
specimen.32G.note: Musculoskeletal baseline: regrowth of multiple phalanges in sequence without malformations. Low inter-individual variability.
specimen.13B.note: Low-generation iguana branch with more efficient behavioural thermoregulation and accentuated dorsal colour shift. Behavioural profile within the norm for the species.
specimen.14C.note: More sensitive parietal eye with better discrimination of polarised light, useful for orientation. Behavioural profile typical of the species.
specimen.23B.note: Accelerated healing of skin wounds and reduced nocturnal heat loss. Basal metabolism optimised for the climate of the Italian greenhouses.
specimen.24C.note: Broadened chromatic visual acuity and greater responsiveness to conspecific gular signals. Marked social interactions but no indicators of self-awareness.
specimen.51B.note: Advanced line close to the 47B branch; ambiguous episodes of prolonged fixation towards the mirror, never reproduced under controlled conditions. Indeterminate behavioural flag, pending validation.
specimen.52C.note: Integrated vision-olfaction sensory map but no cognitive deviation detected. Serves as a negative control against the behaviourally anomalous lines.
specimen.13D.note: Founding elapid with increased resistance to respiratory mycobacterial infections. Higher baseline antibody titre without alterations to venom composition.
specimen.14F.note: Selected for hypoxia tolerance during prolonged brumation; survives long periods at low oxygenation with reduced tissue acidosis.
specimen.23D.note: Faster clearance of gastrointestinal endoparasites. Regular growth and stable reproductive yield, suited to expanding the colony.
specimen.24F.note: Dormancy heart rate reversibly lowerable on thermal command, with full neurological recovery on waking. Reference for transport protocols.
specimen.33D.note: Immune baseline with a broad repertoire of cutaneous antimicrobial peptides. Used to calibrate the pathogen-resistance assays.
specimen.34F.note: Cohort proposed to combine hypoxia tolerance and reduced winter metabolic demand. Under evaluation for effects on fertility.
specimen.71G.note: Mature monitor lizard programme: partial tail regeneration with vertebral bone reconstitution, not just cartilage. Above-average limb muscle mass.
specimen.72F.note: Hypoxia tolerance during prolonged dives with pronounced diving bradycardia. High myoglobin reserves.
specimen.81G.note: Accelerated fracture healing and dense bone remodelling. Candidate for transfer to N10 as a musculoskeletal validation asset.
specimen.82F.note: Transferred out for long-duration controlled metabolic dormancy with full recovery of liver function. Transfer documentation shared with the validation facility.
specimen.92G.note: Occasional problem-solving behaviours in food retrieval, not reliably distinguishable from associative learning. Indeterminate behavioural flag.
specimen.93F.note: Best dormancy efficiency of the Polish programme: reduced energy consumption in seasonal torpor with no measurable muscle loss.
specimen.11E.note: Founding line with more efficient supraorbital salt glands, allowing a stable water balance at high salinities.
specimen.12H.note: Reduced cellular senescence markers and prolonged telomere maintenance. Slow but continuous growth typical of long-lived chelonians.
specimen.21E.note: Hydrophid with an enhanced sublingual salt gland and improved cutaneous oxygen uptake. Stable osmotic balance in full seawater.
specimen.22H.note: Longevity baseline with low tissue oxidative damage and efficient articular cartilage repair.
specimen.31E.note: Cohort proposed to combine robust osmoregulation and tolerance to rapid salinity changes in estuaries. Awaiting assessment of kidney function.
specimen.15B.note: Founding line with finer control of the guanine nanocrystals in the iridophores, broadening the range of colour shift. Faster colour change.
specimen.16C.note: Enhanced independent eye coordination with better distance estimation for tongue projection. Prey-capture accuracy higher than the wild strain.
specimen.25B.note: More stable social colour signalling and better thermal dissipation through dynamic reflectance. Typical territorial behaviour.
specimen.26C.note: Sensory baseline with a broadened panoramic visual field and reduced reaction time to moving stimuli.
specimen.35B.note: Chromatic thermoregulation optimised for the microclimate of the Ugandan greenhouses. Rapid skin healing with faithful restoration of the pigment pattern.
specimen.17C.note: Founding corvid with enhanced visual acuity and eye-beak coordination for tool use. High cognitive performance but within the known repertoire of the wild species.
specimen.18H.note: Extended-longevity line with a low rate of immune senescence. Plumage and liver function stable over multi-year monitoring.
specimen.27C.note: Better auditory discrimination of conspecific vocalisations. Social learning within the norm; no indicators of self-awareness.
specimen.28H.note: Longevity baseline with reduced oxidative stress markers and efficient telomere repair.
specimen.46H.note: Historic fourth-generation iguana line, cryopreserved as a pre-47B reference for the longevity protocol.
specimen.87A.note: Monitor lizard strain archived for high embryonic viability and low perinatal mortality. Starting material for line restoration.
specimen.19A.note: First cryopreserved spider line, used to validate the haemolymph vitrification protocols in arachnids.
specimen.63H.note: Sixth-generation monitor lizard line preserved as a longevity reference predating the more recent strains.
specimen.74G.note: Asset transferred from N6 and validated in the United States for reproducible musculoskeletal regeneration. Bone regrowth and functional recovery independently confirmed.
specimen.86F.note: Specimen validated for controlled metabolic dormancy, transferred from the Polish programme. Torpor and recovery parameters replicated within tolerance.
protocol.A.tratto: Metabolic efficiency, reduction of embryonic mortality
protocol.A.note: Fundamental platform onto which the others are grafted. First generation.
protocol.C.tratto: Extended UV vision, vomeronasal olfaction, thermoception
protocol.D.note: The 'pathogen resistance' branch of the programme.
protocol.E.tratto: Salt glands (inspired by the marine iguana), water retention
protocol.E.note: Adaptation to arid and saline environments.
protocol.F.tratto: Survival at low oxygen levels, controlled metabolic slowdown
protocol.G.tratto: Bone density, strength, regeneration beyond the tail
protocol.H.tratto: Slowed cellular senescence, DNA repair, telomeres
generation.1.testo: High mortality, crude edits. A few robust survivors but cognitively ordinary.
generation.2.testo: First variants of Protocols B and C. An archived specimen with inconclusive behavioural observations that were never replicated; material preserved in the biobank.
generation.3.testo: Best results before the current cohort. Some specimens still active as baseline.
generation.4.testo: The reference brood of the iguana programme. Cognition and behaviour study under way.
generation.5.testo: Generation contemporary with Gen 4; includes specimens unsuitable for standard husbandry and subsequently transferred out.
generation.8.testo: First consolidated line of Laboratory N.6 (Poland).
generation.9.testo: Flagship cohort of the Monitor Lizard programme.
kpi.0.nota: 11 numbered nodes + management, offices, logistics and historic sites
kpi.1.nota: 32 d 14 h 17 min vs ~90 d natural (Iguana iguana)
kpi.3.nota: vs the average of the previous generation
milestone.0.testo: The precision genetics programme is born. First experimental lines on Iguana iguana.
