experiment.exp-n1-crio-vetrificazione-ge: Preserve oocytes and gonadal tissue of at-risk species over the long term without ice crystal formation.
Vitrification with penetrating cryoprotectants (ethylene glycol/DMSO) and ultra-rapid cooling in liquid nitrogen at -196 degrees.
Post-thaw viability of 71% on iguana oocytes, with residual mitochondrial damage still to be reduced.

Background: The long-term preservation of the germplasm of threatened reptiles requires protocols that avoid the nucleation of intracellular ice, the main cause of damage during freezing. Method: Iguana oocytes and fragments of gonadal tissue were vitrified using combined penetrating cryoprotectants (ethylene glycol and dimethyl sulfoxide) at high concentration, with ultra-rapid cooling by direct immersion in liquid nitrogen at -196°C and controlled rapid warming. Post-thaw viability was assessed with membrane integrity assays, mitochondrial membrane potential and metabolic recovery. Results: 71% of the oocytes retained morphological and membrane integrity; however, a significant fraction showed residual mitochondrial depolarisation and high production of reactive oxygen species, indicating oxidative stress that was not fully prevented. Conclusions: Vitrification allows effective ice-free cryopreservation of reptilian germline lines, but reducing mitochondrial damage requires optimisation of the thermal ramps and integration of antioxidants into the cryoprotectant medium.
experiment.exp-n1-archivio-referenza-gen: Build a bank of reference genomes shared across all facilities to track the enhanced lines.
Long-read sequencing (Oxford Nanopore) with de novo assembly and cryptographic indexing of the samples.
214 annotated genomes deposited; some N6 lines show variants not present in the records of origin.

Background: Tracking the enhanced lines across facilities requires complete and verifiable reference genomes. Method: We sequenced 214 multi-species samples with Oxford Nanopore long-read technology, performing de novo assembly (overlap detection and correction, assembly and consensus polishing) and structural and functional annotation; each genome was indexed with cryptographic hashes to guarantee integrity and non-repudiation of the deposits. Results: 214 annotated genomes with chromosome-level continuity were deposited. Comparative analysis revealed, in some lines of facility N6, structural and single-nucleotide variants absent from the records of origin, consistent with undocumented editing or recombination events. Conclusions: The archive provides a shared, tamper-proof reference for genomic surveillance; the discrepancies detected in the N6 lines require cross-checking with the chain of custody and the experimental records.
experiment.exp-n1-stabilita-dna-decennal: Quantify the degradation of archived DNA to define the sample re-verification cycles.
Comparison of fragmentation by capillary electrophoresis on aliquots stored at -80 degrees versus liquid nitrogen over time.
Liquid nitrogen reduces fragmentation by 40% at ten years; -80 degrees remains adequate only under five years.

Background: Defining the re-verification cycles of archived samples requires quantitative estimates of DNA degradation as a function of storage temperature. Method: Aliquots of genomic DNA were stored in parallel at -80°C and in liquid nitrogen; at scheduled intervals, fragmentation was measured by capillary electrophoresis, calculating integrity indices and chain-break rates according to an Arrhenius-type degradation model. Results: At ten years, the liquid nitrogen samples showed fragmentation reduced by about 40% compared with those at -80°C. Storage at -80°C proved adequate within five years, beyond which the accumulation of breaks exceeds the acceptable thresholds for downstream applications. Conclusions: For decade-long archiving and beyond, liquid nitrogen is recommended; for the -80°C samples, five-year re-verification and regeneration cycles are established.
experiment.exp-n1-catena-custodia-campio: Traceability and chain of custody of samples
Guarantee integrity and non-repudiation in the movement of biological materials between sites.
Append-only ledger labelling system with time-stamping and dual-key verification on delivery.
Rolled out to production; two historic provenance discrepancies flagged and being clarified with N9.

Background: The movement of biological materials between sites requires guarantees of integrity and non-repudiation. Method: We implemented a labelling system based on an append-only ledger, in which each custody event is chained by cryptographic hashes and a time-stamp, with dual-key verification on delivery. The integrity of the chain is guaranteed by the computational impossibility of back-dating or altering entries without invalidating the sequence. Results: The system was rolled out to production across all transfers; the automatic comparison between declared provenance and the ledger surfaced two historic provenance discrepancies, now being clarified jointly with facility N9. Conclusions: The adoption of a tamper-proof, time-stamped ledger strengthens traceability and enables the retroactive detection of anomalies; integration with the genomic archive allows cross-checking of sample identity.
experiment.exp-n2-visione-composita.obie: Understand how jumping spiders integrate their eight eyes into a unified, high-resolution visual perception.
experiment.exp-n2-visione-composita.meto: Microscopy and electroretinography with moving stimuli in an arena, tracking the oculomotor response of the principal retinae.
experiment.exp-n2-visione-composita.risu: Identified an active retinal scanning that reconstructs the scene sequentially, not a static frame.
experiment.exp-n2-visione-composita.abst: Background: Jumping spiders (Salticidae) exhibit visual acuity exceptional for their size, mediated by the anterior median (principal) eyes, whose boomerang-shaped retina is organised into four photoreceptor layers served by a long, mobile eye tube. How this architecture, lacking a wide-field fovea, generates a unified perception remains poorly understood. Method: We combined optical microscopy of the eye tube, electroretinography of the principal retinae and the presentation of moving stimuli in an arena, recording the oculomotor responses mediated by the retinal muscles during target tracking. Results: The recordings reveal an active retinal scanning: the principal retina rhythmically sweeps the scene with torsional and lateromedial movements, sequentially sampling contiguous portions of the visual field rather than acquiring a static frame. The temporal integration of these samples, aided by the lateral eyes that detect motion, reconstructs a high-resolution representation. Conclusions: Salticid vision is an active, serial process in which the scene is assembled over time, not captured in an instant, a perceptual model that is economical and consistent with the layered anatomy of the system.
experiment.exp-n2-seta-dragline-ricombin: Increase the tensile strength of the safety silk while preserving its elasticity.
Recombinant expression of spidroins in cell lines and mechanical characterisation by nanoindentation.
Fibres with tenacity 18% higher than the wild strain, but spinning still unstable at scale.

Background: Spider dragline silk owes much of its exceptional tenacity to the major spidroins (MaSp1, MaSp2), repetitive proteins with crystalline poly-alanine blocks and amorphous glycine-rich regions. Recombinantly reproducing fibres with the native balance between tensile strength and elasticity remains a biotechnological challenge. Method: We expressed high-molecular-weight spidroin constructs in heterologous cell lines, purified the proteins and produced fibres by wet spinning; the mechanical properties were characterised with tensile tests and nanoindentation, correlating them with the beta-sheet content assessed spectroscopically. Results: The optimised fibres show tenacity 18% higher than the wild-strain yarn, retaining comparable extensibility thanks to an increased oriented crystalline fraction. However, the spinning process remains unstable at scale, with diameter variability and defects that limit reproducibility. Conclusions: Engineering the terminal regions and the spinning conditions improves tenacity without sacrificing elasticity, but controlling self-assembly remains the bottleneck for industrial production.
experiment.exp-n2-rete-sensoriale-distri: Understand how the web extends the spider's perception beyond its body by transmitting vibrational information.
Laser Doppler vibrometry on the web with controlled sources and spectral analysis of the predatory responses.
The web acts as a tuned mechanical filter that pre-processes the signals before they reach the animal.

Background: Many spiders perceive prey almost exclusively through vibrations transmitted by the silk substrate. The web is not a simple passive medium but a tunable mechanical structure that filters and propagates signals before they reach the mechanoreceptors (slit sensilla) of the legs, extending perception beyond the animal's body. Method: Using laser Doppler vibrometry we measured the transmission of controlled stimuli injected into the web, comparing transverse and longitudinal waves over a wide range of frequencies, and correlating the animal's predatory response with the spectral analysis of the signals arriving at the hub. Results: The web behaves as a tuned mechanical filter: the longitudinal components propagate with less attenuation and retain more directional information, while silk tension and architecture selectively modulate the transmitted bands. The spider adjusts these parameters, pre-processing the information upstream of the nervous system. Conclusions: Vibrational perception is distributed: part of the signal processing is delegated to the material and geometric properties of the web, an example of morphological computation external to the nervous system.
experiment.exp-n2-micro-sorveglianza-bio: Assess the use of setae and ampullae as a model for passive, ultra-low-power vibration detectors.
Reverse engineering of the trichobothria and prototyping of MEMS arrays sensitive to airflow.
The prototype detects movement at two metres; potential dual-use recorded and submitted to internal ethical review.

Background: The trichobothria and slit sensilla of spiders constitute detectors of airflow and vibration with sensitivity close to the thermal limit and negligible energy consumption, since the information is passively transduced by the mechanics of the hair. These organs represent an ideal model for artificial ultra-low-power sensors. Method: We carried out a morphometric and mechanical reverse engineering of the trichobothria, deriving their deflection parameters as a function of flow speed and frequency, and prototyped MEMS arrays with capacitive hairs inspired by that dynamic, testing their response in a controlled-flow wind tunnel. Results: The prototype detects sources of movement up to two metres away with thresholds consistent with the hydromechanical models of the filiform hair, reproducing the directional selectivity observed in nature. The potential dual-use was recorded and submitted to internal ethical review. Conclusions: Passive biomimetic transduction allows highly efficient vibration and flow detectors; the application implications, however, require a responsible assessment of uses.
experiment.exp-n3-rigenerazione-arto-com: Clarify how the blastema reforms a limb with the correct positional identity after amputation.
Cell labelling with fluorescent reporters and longitudinal in vivo imaging during regrowth.
Confirmed the role of the retinoic acid gradient in restoring the proximal-distal axis.

Background: The axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) regenerates complete limbs after amputation, faithfully rebuilding the proximal-distal axis. The blastema cells retain the memory of their original position, but the signals that establish positional identity along the axis remain under study. Method: We labelled cell subpopulations with fluorescent reporters and followed the regrowth by longitudinal in vivo imaging, pharmacologically manipulating the retinoic acid pathway to test its effect on the proximal-distal identity of the regenerate. Results: The imaging confirms that connective tissue cells dominate the blastema, maintaining positional information; exposure to exogenous retinoic acid proximalises the regenerate, inducing structures more proximal than the amputation site, while the endogenous gradient of retinoic signalling proves necessary to restore the correct proximal-distal sequence. Conclusions: The restoration of the proximal-distal axis depends on a gradient of retinoic acid signalling that instructs the positional identity of the blastema cells, consistent with the classic model of retinoid proximalisation and with modern cell-tracking data.
experiment.exp-n3-riprogrammazione-blast: Identify the master genes that trigger cellular dedifferentiation in the wound.
Single-cell RNA-seq on the stump in the first 96 hours post-amputation.
Isolated an early transcriptional signature dominated by immune-response and Wnt genes.

Background: Blastema formation requires that mature cells near the wound re-enter a progenitor programme. Identifying the early molecular signals that trigger this dedifferentiation is crucial to understanding epimorphic regeneration. Method: We performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of the axolotl stump in the first 96 hours post-amputation, reconstructing the transcriptional trajectories of the connective tissue and innate immune populations during blastema activation. Results: The analysis isolates an early transcriptional signature dominated by immune-response genes and Wnt/beta-catenin signalling, with the connective tissue cell types converging towards a relatively homogeneous progenitor state resembling the embryonic limb bud. Macrophage infiltration precedes and accompanies this transition. Conclusions: Blastema activation is a multiphase programme in which immune signals and the Wnt pathway cooperate to reprogram the connective tissue cells towards multipotency, indicating candidate molecular targets for triggering regeneration.
experiment.exp-n3-rigenerazione-cardiaca: Study how the axolotl repairs the heart while avoiding the fibrosis typical of mammals.
Controlled ventricular cryoinjury followed by histology and analysis of cardiomyocyte proliferation.
Functional recovery at 60 days with minimal collagen deposition, antifibrotic mechanism still to be isolated.

Background: Unlike the mammalian heart, which responds to infarction with permanent fibrosis, urodele amphibians regenerate damaged myocardium with minimal scarring. The mechanism rests on the capacity of adult cardiomyocytes to re-enter the cell cycle and proliferate. Method: We induced a controlled ventricular cryoinjury and followed the recovery by histology, quantification of collagen deposition and labelling of cardiomyocyte proliferation, assessing contractile function at 60 days. Results: At 60 days the tissue shows functional recovery with minimal and transient collagen deposition; the repair is sustained by a subpopulation of proliferating cardiomyocytes and by a remodelling of the extracellular matrix mediated by macrophages, without formation of a stable scar. The specific antifibrotic mechanism remains to be isolated. Conclusions: Axolotl cardiac regeneration combines cardiomyocyte proliferation and immune control of fibrosis, in line with what is observed in newts and zebrafish, offering a model for antifibrotic strategies in the mammalian heart.
experiment.exp-n3-crispr-guarigione-cica: Editing of the fibrotic pathway for scar-free healing
Test whether silencing profibrotic pathways extends perfect regeneration to other tissues.
Targeted CRISPR-Cas9 knockout of TGF-beta regulators and comparison of the quality of the repaired tissue.
Reduction of cutaneous scarring, but side effects on the tensile strength of the newly formed tissue.

Background: The axolotl's perfect regeneration is associated with a reduced responsiveness to TGF-beta signalling and a less fibrotic extracellular matrix. Since TGF-beta is a central regulator of scarring, selectively silencing its profibrotic pathways could extend scar-free healing to other tissues. Method: Using CRISPR-Cas9 we performed targeted knockouts of TGF-beta pathway regulators and compared the quality of the repaired skin tissue for collagen architecture, fibronectin and tenascin-C content and tensile properties, relative to unedited controls. Results: Attenuating the profibrotic signalling markedly reduces cutaneous scarring, with a more ordered, dermis-like matrix deposition; however, side effects emerge on the tensile strength of the newly formed tissue, indicating a trade-off between absence of scarring and mechanical integrity. Conclusions: Modulation of the TGF-beta pathway is sufficient to shift repair towards a regenerative phenotype, but restoring the mechanical properties requires fine, balanced control of the signalling, consistent with the role of TGF-beta in regeneration and scarring.
experiment.exp-n4-labirinto-radiale-igua: Spatial memory in a radial-arm maze
Measure the spatial working memory abilities of iguanas in a foraging task.
Eight-arm radial maze with food reward and counting of repeated entries.
The iguanas avoid already-visited arms with 82% accuracy, indicating robust spatial memory.

Background: Spatial working memory, well documented in mammals and birds, was long thought to be limited in reptiles. Recent studies on lizards and tortoises instead indicate robust spatial abilities when rodent paradigms are adapted to the taxon's biology. Method: We tested the iguanas in an eight-arm radial maze with food reward, controlling for olfactory traces and counting repeated entries into already-visited arms as an index of spatial working memory, with analysis of navigation strategies via distal cues. Results: The iguanas avoid already-visited arms with 82% accuracy, well above chance, without relying on olfactory cues, and use distal extramaze cues to orient, indicating the use of a spatial representation rather than a simple response strategy. Conclusions: Iguanas possess robust spatial working memory comparable to that observed in other amniotes, supporting the growing evidence that reptile spatial cognition has historically been underestimated.
Test whether iguanas learn tasks by observing a conspecific demonstrator.
Sliding-door opening test with observer groups versus naive control groups.
Observers solve the task faster, a first hint of social transmission in these reptiles.

Background: Social learning, once thought to be the preserve of social species of mammals and birds, has also been demonstrated in non-social reptiles, challenging the idea that it is an adaptation to group living. Method: We subjected the iguanas to a sliding-door opening task, comparing observer groups, exposed to a conspecific demonstrator, with naive control groups; a ghost control condition isolated the effect of mere stimulus enhancement. Results: Observers solve the task faster and with fewer attempts than naive controls, and the performance is not explained by local enhancement or goal emulation alone, indicating social transmission of information. The effect is modulated by the subjects' age. Conclusions: These results provide a first hint of observational social learning in these reptiles, consistent with the evidence of imitation and behavioural flexibility already reported in other squamates, and suggest that the mechanisms of social learning are evolutionarily ancient.
experiment.exp-n4-autocontrollo-gratific: Assess the iguanas' ability to delay a response for a larger reward.
Delayed-choice task with food quantities increasing as a function of waiting time.
Some individuals tolerate waits of up to 30 seconds, with strong individual variability.

Background: Inhibitory control, the ability to suppress a prepotent response to obtain a delayed benefit, is a central component of executive function. Its comparative basis across vertebrates has been linked to absolute brain size, but data on reptiles remain scarce. Method: We assessed the iguanas in a delayed-choice task, in which the food quantity grew as a function of waiting time, and in a variant of the cylinder task to measure the inhibition of a motor response directed at the reward. Results: Some individuals tolerate waits of up to 30 seconds before responding, with strong inter-individual variability; performance in the cylinder task shows context-specific inhibition and is influenced by learning biases, in line with the moderate levels reported in other squamates. Conclusions: Iguanas exhibit measurable but variable inhibitory control, consistent with the hypothesis that inhibitory capacity scales with brain size and with the context-dependent nature of response inhibition in reptiles.
experiment.exp-n4-riconoscimento-individ: Establish whether iguanas distinguish individuals and remember their past interactions.
Habituation-dishabituation test with olfactory and visual stimuli of known and unknown individuals.
Selective dishabituation response towards new individuals; some subjects show behaviours hard to explain by conditioning alone.

Background: Individual recognition, the basis of dominance hierarchies, territoriality and dear-enemy relationships, has been documented in several lizards that discriminate familiar and unknown conspecifics mainly through chemical cues. Method: We used a habituation-dishabituation paradigm, presenting the iguanas with olfactory and visual stimuli of known and unknown individuals, quantifying the frequency and duration of exploration, in particular the tongue-flicks directed at the scent marks. Results: The subjects show a selective dishabituation response towards new individuals, examining their chemical cues for longer than familiar ones, indicating the ability to recognise individual conspecifics and to remember their identity. Some subjects display behaviours not explainable by associative conditioning alone. Conclusions: Iguanas distinguish specific individuals on the basis of chemical signatures and retain their identity over time, consistent with the evidence of individual recognition mediated by scent marks in squamate reptiles and with the growing re-evaluation of their social cognition.
experiment.exp-n5-proteomica-veleno.obie: Catalogue the toxins of the main laboratory snakes to identify pharmacological targets.
experiment.exp-n5-proteomica-veleno.meto: Tandem mass spectrometry on fractionated venoms and mapping of the active protein domains.
experiment.exp-n5-proteomica-veleno.risu: Identified 47 toxin families, three of them promising candidates as analgesics.
experiment.exp-n5-proteomica-veleno.abst: Aim. To build a comparative catalogue of the toxins of the main laboratory snakes of Eden Exotic (47B universe) in order to identify exploitable pharmacological targets. Method. The venoms were fractionated by RP-HPLC and the individual fractions analysed by tandem mass spectrometry (bottom-up and top-down), with assignment of the toxin families and mapping of the active protein domains through dedicated proteomic databases. Results. 47 recurrent toxin families were resolved, dominated by phospholipases A2, metalloproteases, serine proteases and three-finger toxins; quantitative analysis revealed marked interspecific variability in the abundance profiles. Three low-abundance three-finger peptides showed affinity for pain channels in preliminary assays, emerging as analgesic candidates. Conclusions. Comparative proteomics provides a rational map of venom as a library of bioactive ligands and guides the selection of therapeutic targets, in line with the venomic approach established in the literature.
experiment.exp-n5-peptide-antipertensivo: Develop an antihypertensive derived from the bradykinin-potentiating peptides of the venom.
Peptide synthesis and ACE inhibition assays on cellular and tissue models.
An analogue shows stable inhibition in vitro; in vivo pharmacokinetics still insufficient.

Aim. To develop an antihypertensive candidate derived from the bradykinin-potentiating peptides (BPP) of the venom, exploiting their inhibitory activity on angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). Method. Proline-rich analogues were produced by solid-phase peptide synthesis and assayed for ACE inhibition on tissue preparations and cell lines, with determination of the inhibition constants and assessment of serum stability; pharmacokinetics was estimated in in vivo models. Results. A structurally optimised analogue showed potent and stable ACE inhibition in vitro, with potentiation of the vasodepressor response to bradykinin consistent with the mechanism of the BPPs that led to the development of captopril. The in vivo yield, however, was limited by rapid degradation and insufficient oral bioavailability. Conclusions. Venom confirms its value as a source of scaffolds for ACE inhibitors; pharmacokinetic optimisation remains the main obstacle to therapeutic translation.
experiment.exp-n5-antiveleno-ricombinant: Produce a synthetic antiserum effective against the venoms of multiple species without animal immunisation.
Selection of human antibodies from phage display libraries against recombinant toxins.
Cross-neutralisation of two genera in vitro; efficacy against metalloproteinases still partial.

Aim. To produce a broad-spectrum synthetic antiserum, effective against the venoms of multiple species and free of the recourse to animal immunisation. Method. Representative recombinant toxins (three-finger toxins, long-chain alpha-neurotoxins, metalloproteases) were used as antigens for the selection of human antibody fragments from phage display libraries; the best binders were reformatted as IgG and tested in in vitro neutralisation assays and in murine models. Results. A broadly neutralising human monoclonal antibody blocked alpha-neurotoxins of two elapid genera with cross-neutralisation at a low molar ratio, prolonging the survival of the treated animals. Coverage against the haemorrhagic metalloproteases remained partial, indicating the need for an oligoclonal cocktail. Conclusions. Phage display technology allows safe and reproducible human recombinant antivenoms; extending the spectrum to tissue-acting toxins requires the combination of several complementary antibodies.
Characterise the speed and reversibility of the neuromuscular block induced by alpha-neurotoxins.
Electrophysiology on nerve-muscle preparations and modelling of the receptor-binding kinetics.
Defined the time-effect profile; the dual-use dossier is under restricted review with site N10.

Aim. To characterise the onset speed and reversibility of the neuromuscular block induced by alpha-neurotoxins, in order to define the time-effect profile and the safety margins. Method. Isolated nerve-muscle preparations were used in electrophysiological recordings (voltage clamp and end-plate potentials) during application of short- and long-chain alpha-neurotoxins; the inhibition curves of acetylcholine-induced currents were modelled according to binding kinetics at the muscle nicotinic receptor, estimating association and dissociation constants. Results. The short-chain toxins showed rapid onset with slow, partial recovery of the muscle receptor, while some variants exhibited more marked reversibility. The kinetic model reproduced the observed time-effect profile and the IC50 values in the nanomolar range. Conclusions. A quantitative framework of the neuromuscular block was defined; owing to the dual-use nature of the data, the dossier is submitted to restricted review with site N10 before any further dissemination.
experiment.exp-n6-forza-morso-varani.obi: Quantify the strength and musculoskeletal resistance of the monitor lizards under load.
experiment.exp-n6-forza-morso-varani.met: Force transducers on the bite and high-speed kinematic analysis during predation.
experiment.exp-n6-forza-morso-varani.ris: Recorded a specific force 25% higher than the allometric estimates for the size.
experiment.exp-n6-forza-morso-varani.abs: Aim. To quantify the bite force and musculoskeletal resistance of the monitor lizards under load, combining direct measurements and structural modelling. Method. Force transducers applied to the bite recorded the peaks during voluntary grips, while high-speed videography reconstructed the kinematics of predation; three-dimensional models of the skull derived from tomography were analysed with the finite element method to assess the distribution of stresses during bite and traction. Results. The measured specific force was 25% higher than the allometric estimates for the size; the structural analysis, however, showed that the skull is not optimised for high-absolute-force bites, but rather to withstand the torsional and traction stresses of the grip-and-rip strategy. Conclusions. In monitor lizards, predatory performance depends on the coupling between powerful musculature and a cranial architecture specialised for pulling, rather than on closing force alone, consistent with the known biomechanical models for Varanus.
experiment.exp-n6-resilienza-ipossia.obi: Assess the monitor lizards' resistance to prolonged exertion in low-oxygen environments.
experiment.exp-n6-resilienza-ipossia.met: Treadmill tests in a controlled-oxygen chamber with monitoring of blood lactate.
experiment.exp-n6-resilienza-ipossia.ris: Faster lactate recovery than the controls, thanks to efficient gular-pump ventilation.
experiment.exp-n6-resilienza-ipossia.abs: Aim. To assess the monitor lizards' resistance to prolonged exertion in low-oxygen environments and the mechanisms that sustain their endurance. Method. The animals were subjected to treadmill trials in a controlled-oxygen chamber, with monitoring of ventilation, measurement of maximum oxygen consumption and sampling of blood lactate during exercise and recovery. Results. The monitor lizards maintained a high maximum metabolic rate positively correlated with endurance; under moderate hypoxia, ventilation was sustained by the positive-pressure gular pump, which supplements costal breathing. Lactate recovery was faster than in the controls, consistent with the accessory ventilatory efficiency. Conclusions. The gular pump represents a key adaptation that, by decoupling ventilation and locomotion, mitigates the axial constraint and improves exertion tolerance under reduced oxygen, in agreement with the known physiology of varanids.
experiment.exp-n6-termoregolazione-estre: Determine the operational thermal window within which the monitor lizards retain full motor capacity.
Body-temperature telemetry with locomotion trials at increasing temperatures.
Stable performance up to 40 degrees, with an abrupt drop in coordination beyond the critical threshold.

Aim. To determine the operational thermal window within which the monitor lizards retain full motor capacity and to define the critical threshold of coordination collapse. Method. Body temperature was recorded by telemetry during locomotion trials at increasing temperatures; sprint speed, stride frequency and stride length were measured with videography, and the performance related to thermal performance curves with estimation of the Q10 coefficients. Results. Motor performance remained stable up to about 40 degrees, with low thermal dependence in the preferred range, followed by an abrupt drop in coordination beyond the critical threshold, in agreement with the asymmetric shape of the thermal performance curves. Muscle power proved to be the main limiting factor at high temperatures. Conclusions. Monitor lizards have a broad thermal plateau of full motor efficiency but a narrow margin beyond the optimum, which constrains their use in extreme thermal environments, consistent with the literature on the thermal dependence of locomotion in saurians.
experiment.exp-n6-integrazione-operativa: Load-carrying capacity and operational use under load
Study the sustainable load capacity with a view to supervised operational uses.
Locomotion trials with instrumented harnesses at incremental masses and assessment of fatigue.
Sustainable load up to 15% of body weight; welfare protocol revised after internal objections.

Aim. To study the load capacity sustainable by the monitor lizards and the associated fatigue, with a view to supervised operational uses. Method. The animals walked instrumented courses wearing harnesses with incremental masses; metabolic cost, endurance on a circular track, stride kinematics and lactate recovery were recorded, with parallel assessment of welfare indicators. Results. The load sustainable without compromising locomotion settled at around 15% of body weight; beyond that threshold, endurance dropped rapidly and metabolic cost grew non-linearly, with signs of musculoskeletal fatigue. The high maximum metabolic rate of the varanids nonetheless allowed performance superior to that expected for the size. Conclusions. There is a load threshold beyond which the cost-performance ratio degrades abruptly; in light of the internal objections on animal welfare, the protocol was revised to limit the masses and duration of the trials within conservative physiological margins.
experiment.exp-n7-osmoregolazione-marina: Clarify how sea turtles maintain water balance in hypersaline water.
Measurement of the secretion rate of the lacrimal salt glands under controlled osmotic load.
Excretory capacity higher than estimated, with finer hormonal regulation than expected.

Aim. To clarify how sea turtles maintain their water-salt balance in hypersaline water, quantifying the excretory capacity of the salt glands. Method. Under controlled osmotic load (injection of saline solutions), the secretion rate of the lacrimal salt glands was measured, with determination of the osmotic concentration and the excretion rates of sodium and potassium in the tears; blood parameters such as haematocrit and blood sodium tracked the systemic response. Results. Glandular secretion reached concentrations markedly hypertonic to plasma and seawater, with excretory capacity higher than estimated; the modulation of the response to load appeared to be under finer hormonal control than expected. In the absence of access to seawater, rapid dehydration was observed with an increase in haematocrit and blood sodium. Conclusions. The extrarenal salt glands constitute the primary osmoregulation mechanism of marine reptiles, with a dynamic regulation that exceeds the predictions of the classic models.
Test the use of the geomagnetic field as a map for long-range orientation.
Exposure to simulated magnetic fields in a tank and recording of the swimming direction of the young.
The turtles adjust their course consistently with the simulated latitude, confirming the magnetic map.

Aim. To test whether young sea turtles use the geomagnetic field as a map for long-range orientation, as well as a compass. Method. In a circular tank, the individuals were exposed to magnetic fields replicating the signature (intensity and inclination) of distinct locations along the migratory route; the swimming direction was recorded and analysed with circular statistics to test its consistency with the simulated geographic position. Results. The turtles adjusted their course consistently with the latitude and position simulated by the imposed fields, orienting as if they had to return to the correct migratory trajectory. This confirms the ability to extract bicoordinate positional information from the Earth's field, distinct from simple directional information. Conclusions. The results support the existence of a true magnetic map in marine reptiles, in which geomagnetic elements act as navigation markers, consistent with the established experimental evidence on the loggerhead and on Chelonia mydas.
experiment.exp-n7-longevita-senescenza-t: Identify the cellular mechanisms underlying the very long longevity of marine reptiles.
Analysis of telomere length and oxidative stress in cohorts of very different ages.
Minimal telomere erosion and high antioxidant defences even in the oldest individuals.

Aim. To identify the cellular mechanisms underlying the very long longevity of marine reptiles and to test the hypothesis of negligible senescence. Method. In cohorts of very different ages, telomere length and tissue antioxidant defences were measured, together with markers of oxidative damage; mortality rates and biochemical profiles were compared across age classes to estimate the dynamics of ageing. Results. Telomere erosion proved minimal and constitutive antioxidant defences high even in the oldest individuals, with low oxidative damage. Senescence rates appeared slowed or negligible across much of the sample, though without ruling out a late decline in survival observed in natural populations. Conclusions. The exceptional longevity of the testudines seems sustained by efficient management of oxidative stress and slow telomere attrition, consistent with the comparative evidence that places many species among the organisms with slow or negligible senescence.
experiment.exp-n7-immersione-metabolismo: Understand how tissue function is maintained during prolonged low-oxygen dives.
Heart-rate telemetry and blood-gas sampling during experimental dives.
Deep bradycardia and flow redistribution; some protective pathways prove shared with the axolotl patterns of N3.

Aim. To understand how tissue function is preserved during prolonged low-oxygen dives in marine reptiles. Method. During experimental dives, heart rate and locomotor activity were monitored by telemetry, with serial sampling of blood gases and indicators of anaerobic metabolism; the cardiovascular responses were correlated with dive depth and duration. Results. Deep bradycardia was observed during the longest dives, with a transient fall in heart rate and redistribution of blood flow towards critical organs, protecting the predominantly pulmonary oxygen reserves. Metabolic depression and antioxidant defences limited reoxygenation damage on ascent. Some cytoprotective pathways activated proved shared with the hypoxia-tolerance patterns of the axolotl studied at site N3. Conclusions. The apnea tolerance of marine reptiles combines reflex bradycardia, circulatory redistribution and metabolic suppression, in line with the known mechanisms of resistance to hypoxia and anoxia in reptiles.
experiment.exp-n8-cromatofori-nanocrista: Explain the physical mechanism of rapid colour change in chameleons.
Electron microscopy and spectrophotometry of the chromatophores under controlled stimulation.
Confirmed that the active spacing of the guanine nanocrystals generates the structural colour, not just the pigments.

Background. At facility N8 of Eden Exotic (47B universe) the physical substrate of rapid colour change in chameleons was investigated, distinguishing the contribution of pigments from that of structural colour. Methods. Skin samples from subjects stimulated under controlled conditions were analysed by transmission electron microscopy and reflectance spectrophotometry, correlating the geometry of the guanine nanocrystal lattice in the iridophores with the spectra measured during induced transitions. Results. The colour variation is not explained by pigment dispersion or aggregation alone: the animals actively modulate the spacing between the nanocrystals in the superficial layer of iridophores, shifting the reflectance peak from green-blue to yellow-orange in agreement with photonic crystal theory. A deep layer of iridophores with larger crystals reflects the near-infrared component. Conclusions. Chameleon colour is predominantly structural and under active physiological control; the two-layer model reconciles camouflage, signalling and thermal protection, and provides the mechanistic basis for the behavioural protocols of facility N8.
experiment.exp-n8-mimetismo-adattivo.obi: Measure how rapidly and faithfully chameleons match their livery to the surrounding background.
experiment.exp-n8-mimetismo-adattivo.met: Arenas with variable backgrounds and colorimetric analysis calibrated on predator vision.
experiment.exp-n8-mimetismo-adattivo.ris: Effective matching on natural substrates, less precise on high-contrast artificial patterns.
experiment.exp-n8-mimetismo-adattivo.abs: Background. Facility N8 quantified the speed and fidelity with which chameleons match their livery to the background (background matching), assessing performance from the predators' point of view. Methods. The subjects were exposed in arenas to natural and artificial backgrounds; skin reflectance was recorded with calibrated spectrophotometry and the values projected into colour spaces modelling the vision of avian and snake predators, calculating perceptual distances (JND) between animal and background. Results. On natural substrates (bark, foliage) the matching is rapid and effective, reducing the contrast below the discrimination threshold of the simulated predators within a few minutes. On high-contrast artificial patterns the match remains partial, consistent with the hypothesis that the system is optimised for natural colour statistics. The responses also prove predator-specific. Conclusions. Chameleon camouflage is an active, context-sensitive process, but constrained by the evolved colour repertoire; the results define the operational limits to be considered in the release and reintroduction programmes of facility N8.
experiment.exp-n8-segnalazione-sociale-c: Distinguish the use of colour for camouflage from its use for communication between individuals.
Recording of the colour patterns during territorial encounters with standardised coloured dummies.
The bright colours on the flanks predict the outcome of conflicts, indicating a distinct signalling function.

Background. At N8 it was tested whether chameleon colour change serves, beyond camouflage, for communication between individuals, distinguishing the two functions. Methods. During standardised territorial encounters with calibrated coloured dummies, the colour patterns of the flanks, head and lateral stripes were recorded with multispectral imaging and analysed for luminance, saturation and rate of change, correlating them with the behavioural outcome of the conflict. Results. The bright colours displayed on the flanks and head during escalation predict the outcome of the clashes: individuals that reach greater cephalic brightness and faster colour shift win more frequently, while losers adopt subdued liveries. Different body regions convey distinct information (motivation to approach vs. competitive ability). These signals operate on chromatic and spatial scales different from those used for background matching. Conclusions. Colour in chameleons has a social signalling function distinct from camouflage; the dual function, mediated by the same iridophore apparatus, informs the social management protocols in captivity of facility N8.
experiment.exp-n8-conservazione-reintrod: Assess whether captive-bred chameleons retain the camouflage abilities needed in the wild.
Comparison of colour and antipredator responses between captive and wild subjects under semi-natural conditions.
Captives show slower responses; an environmental enrichment programme launched to bridge the gap.

Background. Facility N8 assessed the reintroduction suitability of captive-bred chameleons, verifying the preservation of the camouflage and antipredator abilities needed in the wild. Methods. Under semi-natural conditions, background colour responses, latency of livery change and antipredator behaviours (immobility, swaying, flight) were compared between captive and wild subjects, with simulated predator stimuli and colorimetric analysis calibrated on predator vision. Results. Captives show slower and less complete colour responses and an attenuated antipredator repertoire compared with wild subjects, consistent with the sensory deprivation and reduced predator exposure typical of the controlled environment. The differences narrow after an environmental enrichment programme with variable substrates and antipredator training. Conclusions. Captivity erodes but does not eliminate camouflage competence; pre-release antipredator conditioning and enrichment are recommended to align the subjects with wild survival standards, in line with the best practices of reintroduction biology adopted by facility N8.
experiment.exp-n9-modello-adattamento-fr: Predict which gene variants favour cold tolerance in ectothermic species.
Machine learning models trained on comparative genomic data and known thermal phenotypes.
The model identifies antifreeze and lipid-metabolism genes with 78% predictive accuracy.

Background: Cold tolerance in ectothermic species depends on molecular adaptations such as antifreeze proteins, ice nucleators and remodelling of lipid metabolism. Method: We trained machine learning models on comparative genomic data and known thermal phenotypes, integrating feature selection and cross-validation to predict the gene variants associated with thermal tolerance. Results: The model reached a predictive accuracy of 78%, assigning predominant weight to genes encoding antifreeze proteins and to pathways of lipid metabolism and the oxidative stress response. The predictions are consistent with the known mechanisms of freeze survival in ectothermic vertebrates. Conclusions: The approach allows the prioritisation of genetic targets for cold tolerance; experimental validation and the expansion of the species set are necessary to reduce overfitting and improve transferability across taxa.
experiment.exp-n9-predizione-effetti-edi: Reduce the off-target effects of CRISPR interventions planned at the other sites.
In silico modelling of the cut sites with neural networks validated on experimental sequencing data.
The prediction reduces off-target cuts by 30% in the experimental designs subjected to verification.

Background: Reducing off-target effects is essential for the safety of the CRISPR-Cas9 interventions planned at the other sites. Method: We modelled in silico the cutting activity of candidate sgRNAs using deep neural networks trained on experimental genome-wide cleavage data, integrating the prediction of on-target efficacy and the off-target profile into a single guide-design workflow. Results: In the experimental designs subjected to verification, model-guided guide selection reduced off-target cuts by 30% compared with guides chosen by conventional criteria, while maintaining on-target efficacy. The predicted off-target sites were confirmed by targeted sequencing. Conclusions: Integrating off-target prediction into guide design reduces the risk of unwanted editing; systematic experimental validation remains necessary, since a fraction of the off-target sites is not captured by computational methods alone.
experiment.exp-n9-atlante-espressione-mu: Integrate the RNA-seq datasets of all the facilities into a single comparative atlas.
Bioinformatics pipeline of batch harmonisation and unsupervised clustering across species.
Conserved expression modules for tissue repair emerged across axolotls, turtles and monitor lizards.

Background: The integration of the RNA-seq datasets generated by the different facilities is hampered by technical and biological batch effects. Method: We built a harmonisation pipeline that corrects batch effects through identification of mutual nearest neighbours and projection into a shared latent space, followed by unsupervised clustering and comparison of the expression modules across species. Results: The integrated atlas allowed cells to be grouped by cell type rather than by dataset of origin. Conserved expression modules associated with tissue repair emerged, shared across axolotls, turtles and monitor lizards, suggesting a common regenerative transcriptional programme. Conclusions: The comparative atlas provides a resource for the cross-species study of regeneration; the interpretation of the conserved modules requires functional validation and attention to the limits of orthology between distant taxa.
experiment.exp-n9-anomalie-neurali-emerg: Search for unexpected genomic correlates associated with cognitive behaviours not foreseen by the enhancement designs.
Association analysis between variants and behavioural phenotypes reported by the sites, with rigorous statistical control.
Weak but recurrent signal on neural development pathways; interpretation deliberately limited pending replication.

Background: The search for unexpected genomic correlates associated with unforeseen cognitive behaviours requires rigorous statistical control to avoid false positives. Method: We conducted association analyses between genetic variants and behavioural phenotypes reported by the sites, applying estimation of the genetic component of variance, correction for population structure and correction for multiple testing. Results: A weak but recurrent signal emerged on neural development pathways; the effect size is modest and the significance at the limit of the corrected thresholds. In keeping with the known fragility of results at low statistical power, the interpretation was deliberately limited. Conclusions: The signal warrants an independent replication with larger samples and standardised phenotyping before any causal inference; at present the results are considered hypothesis-generating and not conclusive.
experiment.exp-n10-validazione-campo-pro: Field validation of the enhancement protocols
Verify that the traits enhanced in the laboratory hold up under real operational conditions.
Standardised trials in controlled external environments with repeated measurement of key performances.
Most traits hold up; some performances drop under unforeseen environmental stress.

Background: The traits enhanced in the laboratory must be validated under real operational conditions to verify their stability. Method: We carried out standardised trials in controlled external environments, with repeated measurements of key performances, pre-registered protocols and analysis plans and adequate statistical power to limit non-replicable results. Results: Most traits were maintained within the expected ranges; some performances, however, decreased under unforeseen environmental stress, highlighting a context sensitivity not captured by the laboratory conditions. Conclusions: Field validation confirms the overall robustness of the protocols but identifies critical environmental factors to be incorporated into the predictive models; pre-registration and standardisation of the measurements proved decisive for the soundness of the conclusions.
experiment.exp-n10-sigma-integrazione-op: Define the boundaries of responsible use of the dual-use lines in real application scenarios.
Case study with a risk matrix, independent ethical review and predefined stopping criteria.
Three authorisation levels defined; two proposals rejected by the committee for disproportionate risk.

Background: The use of dual-use lines in real application scenarios requires boundaries of responsible use defined in advance. Method: The Sigma Programme adopted a structured case study with a risk matrix, independent ethical review and predefined stopping criteria, in line with the international frameworks for the governance of dual-use research. Results: Three levels of authorisation for use were defined, graded according to the risk-benefit ratio and the reversibility of the interventions. The ethics committee rejected two proposals for risk deemed disproportionate to the expected benefit. Conclusions: A transparent decision-making process, with explicit thresholds and stopping criteria, allows the supervised operational integration of the dual-use lines; independent review and the documentation of rejected decisions are essential elements of accountability and traceability.
experiment.exp-n10-riproducibilita-cross: Establish whether the results of the individual facilities replicate with independent protocols and instruments.
Blind replication of selected experiments with teams and equipment different from the original.
68% of the studies replicated; the discrepancies concentrate on subjective behavioural measures.

Background: The credibility of the results of the individual facilities depends on their replicability with independent protocols and instruments. Method: We selected a sample of experiments and attempted their blind replication, with teams, equipment and reagents different from the original, pre-registering protocols and analyses. Results: 68% of the selected studies were replicated. The discrepancies concentrated on the subjective behavioural measures, while the objective molecular and physiological measures showed the greatest stability. The effect size in the replications was on average smaller than the original. Conclusions: The replication rate is in line with what is observed in large reproducibility projects in the biomedical field; the standardisation of behavioural measures and the systematic adoption of pre-registration are recommended to reduce variability across sites.
experiment.exp-n10-quadro-etico-dual-use: Build a transparent process for assessing the risks and benefits of the dual-use lines.
Delphi method with internal and external experts and definition of shared acceptability thresholds.
Adopted as a company standard; documented disagreements remain on the weight to give to remote risks.

Background: The assessment of the risks and benefits of the dual-use lines requires a transparent and shared decision-making process. Method: We applied a Delphi method with internal and external experts, iterating questionnaires with controlled feedback until shared acceptability thresholds and explicit criteria for reporting consensus were defined. Results: The process produced a decision framework adopted as a company standard, with graded acceptability thresholds and an obligation to document decisions. Documented disagreements remain on the weight to attribute to remote risks, of low probability but high impact. Conclusions: The Delphi method provides a structured and reproducible path for expert consensus on dual-use research, consistent with the international governance frameworks; the transparent recording of residual disagreements is an integral part of decision-making accountability.
experiment.exp-n11-mimica-vocale-corvidi: Study the ability of corvids and parrots to imitate and reproduce novel sounds.
Exposure to controlled acoustic stimuli and spectrographic analysis of the vocalisations produced.
Faithful reproduction of complex phonemes within a few weeks, with long-term retention.

Background. Facility N11 of Eden Exotic (47B universe) studied the ability of corvids and parrots, both open-ended vocal learners, to imitate and reproduce novel sounds. Methods. The subjects were exposed to controlled acoustic stimuli (synthetic phonemes and heterospecific vocalisations) on a repeated schedule; the productions were acquired and compared with the models through spectrographic analysis, spectro-temporal similarity measures and retention tests over a span of weeks. Results. Both taxa faithfully reproduce complex phonemes within a few weeks, with progressive improvement in similarity and stabilisation of the learned template; long-term retention is high even in the absence of continuous reinforcement. The vocal flexibility is consistent with the vocal-learning continuum that unites songbirds, parrots and humans. Conclusions. The corvids and parrots of facility N11 show open-ended vocal learning and robust acoustic memory, prerequisites for the subsequent experiments on individual signatures, referentiality and cultural transmission of the repertoires.
experiment.exp-n11-firma-vocale-identita: Test whether birds use distinctive calls as labels to identify specific individuals.
Recording and automatic classification of the calls with acoustic models and playback tests.
Stable name-calls identified; individuals respond selectively to their own signature.

Background. Facility N11 tested whether birds use distinctive calls as vocal labels to identify specific individuals. Methods. The contact calls of a marked population were recorded and classified with automatic acoustic models; playback tests measured the subjects' selective response to their own signature and to those of known and unknown conspecifics, assessing latency, orientation and response vocalisation. Results. Stable individual vocal signatures, learned during development, were identified; the subjects respond selectively to their own label and show vocal matching during interactions, imitating the call of the addressed individual. This use of learned vocal labels to address specific individuals recalls phenomena documented in wild parrots and bottlenose dolphins. Conclusions. The birds of facility N11 possess a system of vocal identity based on learned and shared signatures, which acts as an individual name within the social network; the result underpins the subsequent referential communication tests.
experiment.exp-n11-comunicazione-referen: Determine whether the calls can refer to specific objects or events in the context.
Object exchange and request tasks with a learned association between vocalisation and referent.
Some subjects request the correct object with dedicated calls; robustness still under verification.

Background. Facility N11 assessed whether vocalisations can refer to specific objects or events in the context, that is, whether they support referential communication. Methods. In object exchange and request tasks, the subjects learned associations between dedicated vocalisations and referents; the accuracy of requesting the correct object, generalisation to new exemplars and robustness in random arrays were measured, with controls for non-referential associative learning. Results. Some subjects request the correct object by emitting dedicated calls and generalise to new exemplars, indicating a functionally referential use of the signal analogous to the vocal labelling documented in grey parrots and to the semantic communication of alarm calls. Robustness remains variable across individuals and under statistical verification. Conclusions. The vocal repertoire of the birds of facility N11 can encode external referents beyond the emotional state of the signaller, although full referentiality requires further controls; the results place these taxa within the framework of animal referential communication.
experiment.exp-n11-cultura-vocale-trasmi: Observe how vocal repertoires spread and change across groups over time.
Longitudinal acoustic monitoring of groups with analysis of call similarity networks.
Documented the spread of vocal variants between individuals, with drifts reminiscent of local dialects.

Background. Facility N11 observed how vocal repertoires spread and change across groups over time, looking for evidence of cultural transmission and dialect formation. Methods. A longitudinal acoustic monitoring of stable groups collected thousands of calls; the networks of acoustic similarity between individuals and over time were reconstructed with automatic classification, tracking the appearance and spread of vocal variants and their drift. Results. The spread of vocal variants between socially connected individuals is documented, with convergence within subgroups and divergence between separate groups, producing drifts reminiscent of local dialects. Transmission follows social rather than genetic routes, consistent with the cultural vocal learning described in songbirds and wild parrots. Conclusions. The vocal repertoires of facility N11 are learned, dynamic and socially structured traditions; the emergence of dialects provides an experimental model for studying the cultural evolution of communication and informs the management of the groups in captivity.
company.claim: Everything measured, everything monitored, everything under control.
company.descrizione: Eden Exotic designs and breeds genetically enhanced organisms through a network of specialised facilities around the world. Precision genomics, controlled breeding and the study of behaviour for specimens that are more resilient, more stable and quicker to mature. Every enhanced characteristic amplifies a trait already present in nature: we do not invent, we accelerate.
company.settore: Biotechnology · Genetic engineering · Adaptive biological systems
company.principi: One single standard, three operating climates: cold, temperate, extreme.
Real, verified science: no undocumented shortcuts.
Amplify, not invent: every enhancement extends an existing natural trait.
Total traceability: documented CITES compliance on every specimen.
Only what the data support: no promise beyond the evidence.
mission.statement: To build adaptable and resilient biological systems — capable of thriving where ordinary life struggles — through rigorous, measurable and responsible genetic engineering.
mission.visione: A future in which biological resilience is designable: for species conservation, for hostile environments, for research and for civil defence.
mission.dualUse: Part of our research is dual-use (civil and defence) in nature. We treat it with seriousness: stated purposes, dedicated oversight and the conviction that a technology is not good or bad in itself, but for the use one chooses to make of it.

Big goals, verifiable steps. Generations are our unit of progress.
Dual-use treated as such: legitimate purposes, strict control, total traceability.
The specimens are subjects of study, not mere paperwork. Welfare and dignity documented.
What is not ready is not announced. Discretion protects the research and those who work on it.

person.erik-sorensen.ruolo: Head of the redundant archive · ARCH
person.erik-sorensen.bio: Directs the redundant archive in Svalbard, dedicated to backup preservation and data recovery of the biobank. Defines the redundancy policies and the data restoration protocols. Oversees the long-term integrity and availability of the archives.
person.erik-sorensen.voce: Methodical and forward-thinking, he reasons in terms of failure and recovery scenarios.
person.erik-sorensen.background: Data management specialist with experience in long-term backup archives.
person.ingrid-halvorsen.ruolo: Cryopreservation and data infrastructure technician · ARCH
person.ingrid-halvorsen.bio: Technician of the Svalbard archive, handles the cryopreservation of samples and the management of the data infrastructure. Monitors the preservation parameters and the maintenance of the storage systems. Records and verifies backup and restore operations.
person.ingrid-halvorsen.voce: Precise and reliable, she keeps every preservation parameter under control.
person.ingrid-halvorsen.background: Laboratory technician with experience in cryopreservation and data storage systems.
person.paulo-ribeiro.ruolo: Head of the field station · FIELD
person.paulo-ribeiro.bio: Directs the Manaus field station, dedicated to the collection and study of wild lines in the Amazon. Coordinates the field campaigns, the collection permits and the relations with local bodies. Oversees the traceability of samples according to CITES standards.
person.paulo-ribeiro.voce: Pragmatic and attentive, he adapts the plans to field conditions.
person.paulo-ribeiro.background: Field biologist with extensive experience in the Amazon and in the management of research stations.
person.beatriz-alves.bio: Field biologist at the Manaus station, she handles the collection, monitoring and initial characterization of the wild lines. Oversees the temporary housing of the samples and the recording of field data. Supports the logistics of the campaigns and the preservation of the materials.
person.beatriz-alves.voce: Attentive and systematic, she notes every observation carefully in the field.
person.beatriz-alves.background: Biologist with experience in herpetological surveys and field work in tropical environments.
